News.title: Gloomy UK to be soaked in rain this week after record-breaking summer – but Met Office forecasts more heatwaves to come
News.content:
RAIN CHECK Gloomy UK to be soaked in rain this week after record-breaking summer – but Met Office forecasts more heatwaves to come

THE UK is set to be soaked in rain this week after a record-breaking summer – but the Met Office says more heatwaves could be coming.

Rain is sweeping the UK after a spell of dry weather, with nearly three-quarters of England and the entirety of Wales facing drought.



It comes after the UK saw temperatures reach highs of 38C in the country’s fifth heatwave of the year last week, which saw a rare amber alert for heat issued across the nation.

However, the Met Office has predicted an increased amount of rain making its way across the country this week alongside breezier conditions.



From Monday onwards, the north will see cloud and outbreaks of heavy rain which will gradually move southward introducing “fresher conditions” with showers more widespread on Thursday.

But the national forecaster says the hot weather could return with the potential for a sixth heatwave before the UK’s summer comes to an end.



The forecast, from August 30 to September 13, says: “There is a chance that late-season hot spells or heatwaves develop, especially in the south.”

It’s predicted the UK will see “drier, more settled weather, slightly more likely towards the south and east”.



Temperatures during this period are “again likely to be near to or above average overall”.

From next Friday to the end of the month, the Met Office says Brits are likely to see a changeable period.

Many parts of the UK may see showers or longer spells of rain with the possibility of some drier weather in between as high pressure sweeps across the country.

However, low pressure systems from the Atlantic “could lead to a period of widespread rain and strong winds at times” with the chance for some thunderstorms.

The Met Office added: “Temperatures are more likely to be above normal than below overall, though the possibility of widespread or exceptional heat is lower than in recent weeks.”



This chance of rainfall comes as two thirds of the country face drought status as a result of consistently dry conditions.

According to the National Drought Group, England faced its driest July since records began 190 years ago, with parts of Hampshire, the Isle of Wight and West Sussex not experiencing rain for over two months.

In response to the drought and the dry conditions, over 27million Brits currently face hosepipe ban restrictions.

These have been enforced by nine water companies to prevent unnecessary water use.

No water company has confirmed when the restrictions will end, but it is anticipated for when water levels are replenished.



Thursday marked the second time that the UK has hit 38C in 2026, with the previous high of exactly 38C recorded in June in Lingwood, Norfolk.

The Met Office said: “The only other time this has happened twice in one year was in 2022. It also makes it the 5th hottest day on record.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

However, as Brits flocked to the beach, some regions have had cooler weather, with Scotland and Northern Ireland seeing wetter conditions.

Record-breaking heatwaves in May and June led to more than 2,800 excess deaths, with the PM urging the public to check in on vulnerable relatives and friends during the extreme heat.

News.title: Miraculous moment bloodied fighter pilot walks away from fiery F-18 crash after jet slammed into mountainside
News.content:
THIS is the miraculous moment a stunned marine fighter pilot walked up to sheriff deputies after surviving a fiery F-18 crash.

His jet slammed into a mountainside in Rimrock, Washington, on June 13 during a training exercise.



Now, the Yakima County Sheriff’s Office has released the bodycam footage showing the lucky-to-be-alive pilot approaching officers moments after the crash.

The unidentified pilot assigned to Marine Aircraft Group 11, 3rd Marine Aircraft Wing in Miramar, California, managed to eject and deploy his parachute before slamming into trees.



In the clip, he is seen calmly walking down the road to deputies with blood across his face, confirming he was the only pilot while also being on the phone to 911.

“I can see parachute lacerations,” the deputy said, before the dazed pilot confirmed, “Yeah, looks like I went through some trees on the way down.”

The jet slammed into the mountainside sending a plume of black smoke into the sky and sparking a wildfire.

The officer told colleagues on radio that fire teams had been deployed to the scene before asking the pilot what kind of aircraft it was.



“That’s an F- well, that was an F-18,” he replied.

“We were doing circles over the lake, doing some low-level training and then I tucked in, and I’m not sure exactly…honestly, I’m a little frazzled.”

“You hit the tree bad, bud,” a witness told the injured pilot in the clip.



“I went through the trees,” the pilot added.

Later, he was filmed making a phone call in which he calmly said, “Hey, buddy, I just crashed,” with video showing his parachute hanging from a tree.

Officials confirmed that he suffered minor lacerations to his face and that there had been a “non-fatal aviation mishap.”

An investigation into the crash is still underway and the pilot has not been named.

News.title: Blood-drinking ‘vampire’ animal killer terrorised our village with severed heads & creepy occult rituals
News.content:
A SELF-PROCLAIMED vampire slaughtered animals and scattered their remains around a village in a seven-month reign of terror.

Married dad Benjamin Lewis – who believed he would never die if he drank blood – terrorised villagers by dumping “maimed and disfigured” carcasses everywhere.



Dead deer and lambs were left in and around churches and tied to flagpoles in the New Forest, Hampshire, prompting fears of satanism.

The twisted 48-year-old – who was in a cult – was obsessed with vampires and satanism, with a collection of Twilight books discovered at his home.





He injured animals as a child but this rapidly escalated to murdering and disfiguring lambs and deer.

A psychiatrist said he feared Lewis could even go on to harm humans after the animal-killer tried to attack him on a visit.

Speaking to The Sun, terrorised locals described life in the shadow of his twisted activities at the satanism hotspot as “ghastly” and “horrific”.

Lewis stole lambs from two small Hampshire farms in the dead of night, cut their throats and dumped their bodies at four churches.



Sarah Harrison was left heartbroken after sheep were stolen from Parsonage Farm in the tiny village of Bramshaw.



Tiny lambs that were just days old, costing £180 each, had their necks cut and then hung from a flagpole at St Peter’s Church.

She said: “It was horrific, what he did. I don’t want to talk too much about it, I just want to be done with it, but it was awful.

“It wasn’t about the cost for me though, it was the lives of those poor lambs, it was horrible.”

She said she was scared to walk alone at night and had thought about leaving the New Forest, though her family had lived there for generations.

“I’m wondering what will it be next. When I hear a sound outside I think is that him.”



Cops carried out surveillance on religious sites on significant dates in the satanic calendar as they tried to trap Lewis.

Mixed animal blood was found in his car when he was arrested.

Officers found satanic symbols, ritual notes and sick poems when they raided his home.



There were also drawings of vampires and “concerning books about vampires and how best to kill humans”.

A suitcase containing crosses and pictures of “people cutting and sucking blood from each other” were also discovered.

During a court appearance, Lewis, from Southampton, answered “Count Dracula” when asked to identify himself.

The court heard he dumped a headless deer at Christ Church, Emery Down, in February 2025.

Two weeks later he put the head in the pulpit on top of a cross.



He also put a deer head on the gates at Anchor House, where he was receiving psychiatric treatment.

“Count Dracula” also put a dead lamb up a flagpole with a tarot card next to it.

Another deer’s head “crawling with maggots” was horrifically discovered on a pew.

A second lamb was put on a tree stump with an inverted stone cross next to it at Christ’s Church in Colbury.



The court was told Lewis left a dead frog on a cross in church at just 13 years old.

The animal carcasses were found at Anchor House, Christ Church in Colbury, St Peter’s Church in Bramshaw, St Theresa’s Church in Totton and Christ Church in Emery Down – with “distressed” kids stumbling upon the bodies.

The New Forest is famous for witchcraft, satanism and all things occult.

The beauty spot’s village of Burley even housed a supposed white witch named Sybil Leek.



Lewis – who called himself “Count Dracula” in court – was first arrested in 2003 for terrorising a vicar and his family in the area.

He was locked up after pretending to be a vampire, making abusive phone calls and posting obscene pictures on the church noticeboard.

The 48-year-old was part of a group making howling noises from a graveyard near the vicarage.

Southampton Crown Court heard Lewis believed drinking blood would prolong his life.

He believed that if he drank enough blood, he wouldn’t go to hell and would become a vampire instead.



But his vile antics left locals so terrified they stopped going to church – including a mum who was too scared to visit her son’s grave.

Roger Sloley, 87, is a retired schoolteacher who has been visiting St Peter’s Church in Bramshaw every Sunday for 40 years.

He is also on the church committee, and said they considered getting CCTV for the church because of the “horrible crimes”.



He said: “It’s clear he’s obviously a nutjob. What he did was horrible.

“He stole sheep from the farm just up the road – I feel bad for the farmer.

“The church committee were thinking of getting CCTV. In the end we couldn’t afford it but they were scared.

“It wasn’t the only time something like that happened in the church. We also had loads of gravestones broken and knocked over. The church seems to attract it.

“I don’t know why he did it but it was ghastly.”



There are a number of occult-themed shops in the area – which Lewis used to frequent.

A member of staff at The Coven of Witches, who wanted to remain anonymous, said that he used to come in and buy strange paraphernalia for his rituals.

She said: “He used to come in here quite a lot. He would always wear a long black trench coat.

“He actually seemed pretty normal – you wouldn’t think anything of it – but it’s a bit weird to think that he came in here.

“He would buy candles and things, I suppose to use for whatever he was doing.”



Another member of staff added: “We don’t even sell ouija boards here.

“We’re all about crystals and healing.”

Lewis was given an indefinite hospitalisation order at Southampton Crown Court, Hampshire, on August 4.



He pleaded guilty to stealing lambs on two occasions and admitted five charges of religiously aggravated harassment from February to August in 2025.

Psychiatrist Dr Gauruv Malhan told the court Lewis had autism and personality disorders, and saw himself as belonging to a vampire cult.

Over the years, a spate of killings and chilling iconography has sparked suspicion among some that a Satanic cult was operating in the New Forest.

A black cat with a gouged-out eye was strung up on a flag pole at St Peter’s Church in Bramshaw.

‘666’, the number of the Devil, and a pentagram were also graffitied on the historic building during the un-Godly attack.



The pentagram is a five-sided star used in Pagan religions but an inverse version is known as the Sigil of Baphomet, Satanism’s motif – they also use an inverse crucifix.

In 2020, sheep were discovered skewered by spears, faces spray painted with Satanic symbols, lying next to a upside down crucifix made of hay.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Police investigating the 2019 killings in Cadnam and Bradshaw brought in the Pagan Police Association to unravel the mystery.

A 41-year-old man from Winchester was arrested but later released.

News.title: Should more be done to stop benefit scroungers from splashing out on holidays? VOTE NOW
News.content:
POLL OF THE DAY Should more be done to stop benefit scroungers from splashing out on holidays? VOTE NOW

BENEFIT scroungers are swapping Britain for sun loungers as they splash out on holidays abroad.

Every year, scores of holidaymakers are jet-setting on foreign getaways with money in their pockets, thanks to our generous welfare system.



The Sun reported how an out-of-work benefits’ dad splurged £1,000 on a Benidorm getaway – his second holiday in a month.

It formed part of an investigation into the so-called “Costa del Dole” after it was revealed thousands of expats are claiming disability benefits while living overseas.



Statistics show 2,244 people are on Personal Independence Payment (PIP) despite residing in countries such as Spain, Italy, Portugal and France.

The Department of Work and Pensions is shelling out up to £10million a year on the expats, and the number claiming has shot up by 86 per cent since before the pandemic.



A Benidorm whistleblower claimed some are getting rich off fraudulent claims and spending the money on Botox and all-day boozing sessions.

Critics say that if current trends continue, the benefit issue is set to bankrupt Britain.

News.title: Body found near river in search for mum, 66, last seen outside Cotswolds hotel 10 days ago
News.content:
'ABSOLUTELY DEVASTATED' Body found near river in search for mum, 66, last seen outside Cotswolds hotel 10 days ago

THE body of a woman who was last spotted outside a hotel 10 days ago has been found near a river.

Cops said Caroline Heininger, 66, was found dead near the River Windrush in Burford, Oxfordshire, on August 15.



She was reported missing on August 5, after she was last seen on CCTV wearing beige trousers and a hoody outside Burford Lodge at about 5.30am.

Police launched an immediate search, deploying 200 officers and sending out multiple helicopters.



However, the rescue operation was brought to a tragic close yesterday after cops discovered a body thought to belong to Caroline near the river.

A spokesperson for Thames Valley Police said: “We have some very sad news to bring you.



“Officers searching for a missing woman, Caroline from Burford, have sadly found a body near to the River Windrush, Burford this morning.

“The discovery was made following extensive searches by our officers and volunteers from Lowland Rescue Oxfordshire.”

They added that formal identification had not yet taken place, but the body was believed to belong to the 66-year-old.

Her next of kin has been informed.



They continued: “We would like to thank the community who came together to share the appeals for Caroline.

“We would also like to thank Lowland Rescue Oxfordshire for their support in assisting our officers with searches since Caroline was reported missing.”

Her death is currently being treated as unexplained but not suspicious.

Hundreds of residents responded to the cops’ appeal, with locals organising search groups amongst themselves.

Caroline’s family also released a message during the operation, wishing for her “safe return home”.



They said: “We would like to express their deepest gratitude to everyone who has contributed to the search efforts so far and would encourage anyone who has information to come forward.”

Since the tragic discovery, messages of condolences have been shared on social media.

News.title: Man, 55, dies after being bitten by ‘out of control’ dog as owner arrested on suspicion of murder
News.content:
A 55-YEAR-OLD man has died after being bitten by an “out of control” dog as the owner is arrested on suspicion of murder.

Cops scrambled to the scene after reports that a man was attacked by a German Shepherd after an altercation on a footpath in Wakefield, West Yorkshire.



He was rushed to hospital yesterday afternoon but sadly passed away from critical injuries some hours later.

Police have arrested a 55-year-old man on suspicion of murder and owning a dog dangerously out of control in a public space causing injury.



The man remains in police custody, with cops also seizing the German Shepherd that was involved.

Anyone with information that could help the probe is urged to contact West Yorkshire Police.



A spokesperson for the force said: “An investigation has been launched into the death of a man following an altercation in the Calder Grove area of Wakefield yesterday afternoon (Saturday 15 August).

“The man’s death is being investigated by the Homicide and Major Enquiry Team and detectives are making an appeal for any witnesses to come forward, particularly two people who stopped to assist the injured man.



“Police received calls from 1.36pm reporting an altercation that had taken place a short time earlier on the old trainline footpath off Blacker Lane during which a man had been bitten by a dog.

“The 55-year-old man was taken to hospital in a critical condition and died shortly after 7pm last night.

“A 55-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of murder and being the owner of a dog dangerously out of control in a public place causing injury and is currently in custody.



“A dog, which is understood to have been the one involved in this incident, has been seized by police.”

Detective Chief Inspector Michael Cox added: “Sadly, a man has died and it is really important that we understand the circumstances of what has taken place.

“We know that two people, one named Sophie, stopped to assist the injured man and direct officers. We would urge these two people to come forward to help us with our ongoing enquiries into this tragic incident.

“The initial altercation has happened in an area used by walkers and we are urging anyone who has potentially seen or heard any part of the exchange between these two men to please make contact.”

News.title: Locals urged to report dodgy vape shops & barbers in high street crackdown
News.content:
DODGY vape shops and barbers on the High Street must be ‘shopped’ over suspicions of tax fraud, the Chancellor says.

John Healey is urging the public to provide the “eyes and ears” for the taxman if they suspect these firms are breaking the law and blighting shopping areas.



Ministers have beefed-up the Report Tax Fraud system making it even easier to raise the alarm if something doesn’t look right. Information can be submitted anonymously.

The Chancellor, walking down a high street in his South Yorkshire constituency, said: “The people who know best are those who live locally.”



He added: “If you think there is a particularly dodgy business that might be dodging tax, here’s a way you can report it directly.”

The public will be asked to give specific information they have observed such as suspicious activity, locations and timings to do with money laundering or any other attempts to defraud the taxman.

He added: “It’s a way for us to pick up leads that might help us deal with tax fraud and businesses that aren’t paying their way but are also some of those that might be blighting the high streets for the future.

“Too many high streets have been blighted by dodgy shops that harm local communities and undercut honest businesses.

“If you see something that doesn’t look right, like suspected tax fraud or money laundering, use HMRC’s fraud reporting service and help protect our high streets.”

HMRC are expected to carry out more than 30,000 interventions this year to tackle the issue as part of an enforcement blitz.



PM Andy Burnham this week said town centres had been hollowed out after decades of decline and that town halls will receive more powers over the firms that open.

The public can report tax fraud by clicking on this government link

News.title: People who fled Stourbridge fires start to return home
News.content:
People who had to flee their houses during the devastating Stourbridge fires are starting to return home, as a firefighter said it was "a miracle no one has died".

Many families are only just discovering the extent of damage to their homes as West Midlands Fire Service allowed some behind the cordon after three days.

Nineteen properties across five streets have been fully destroyed with another 18 severely damaged.

Aerial images of the scene appear to show some houses have remained entirely intact while those next to them have been burnt to the ground.

Residents of Brunswick Gate, Landsgate, Ounty John Lane, Quarry Park Road and Racecourse Lane were asked to gather to speak to fire chiefs one by one.

They then learned if it was safe to return or if their home needed significant repairs or had been lost entirely.

A West Midlands firefighter who wished to remain anonymous told the BBC he had "never prayed for rain so much".

"All I can say is in 23 years I've never seen anything like it," he said.

"We have not stopped - no food, no rest, it's onto the next [fire].

"Fire spreads so, so fast and it's a miracle that no one has died."

The blaze in Stourbridge was one of several that broke out across England and Wales on Thursday, the hottest day of the year so far.

Phil Garrigan from the National Fire Chief's Council (NFCC) said on Saturday that 11 major fires in the past 48 hours and 43 new wildfires since Friday have left services under "incredible pressure".

News.title: Murder inquiry after man bitten by dog dies
News.content:
A murder inquiry has begun after the death of a man who was bitten by a dog on a footpath in West Yorkshire.

The 55-year-old was injured in an altercation on a disused railway line off Blacker Lane in Calder Grove, Wakefield, at about 13:30 BST on Saturday. He was taken to hospital in a critical condition but died just after 19:00.

West Yorkshire Police has appealed for two people, one of whom is called Sophie, who stopped to help the injured man to come forward.

A force spokesperson said a 55-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of murder and of being the owner of a dog dangerously out of control in a public place, causing injury. He remains in custody.

The dog believed to have been involved in the incident has been seized by officers.

Det Ch Insp Michael Cox said: "Sadly, a man has died and it is really important that we understand the circumstances of what has taken place.

"We know that two people, one named Sophie, stopped to assist the injured man and direct officers."

He added: "We would urge these two people to come forward to help us with our ongoing inquiries into this tragic incident.

"The initial altercation happened in an area used by walkers and we are urging anyone who has seen or heard any part of the exchange between these two men to please make contact."

News.title: Reform proposes £50bn welfare bill cut with changes to disability payments for millions
News.content:
Reform UK says it would aim to cut about Â£50bn from the benefits bill and scrap the disability payments system, Pip, if it comes in to government.

Robert Jenrick, the party's treasury spokesperson, said the plans, to be set out in full on Monday, would be the most comprehensive overhaul to the welfare system in a generation and affect nearly three million people.

In an article for the Sunday Telegraph, external he said the current system is "suicidal empathy" and "a strange perversion of compassion".

Labour said it was "fantasy economics, built on stripping support from disabled people", while the Conservatives called it a "half-baked policy" and another "attempt to distract from" questions about the Â£5m gift party leader Nigel Farage received.

Reform's plans include making companies pay for any employees off sick for the first two years. Businesses with more than five employees would have to take out insurance to cover the cost.

Reform says this is modelled on the Dutch system and would incentivise employers to make adaptions and encourage people back to work to reduce their insurance premiums.

The party says they would cut the National Insurance contributions (NICs) paid by employers to offset the cost of this measure, insisting the change would be cost neutral for businesses.

In a policy document to be published next week, which the BBC has seen an extract of, the party estimates 2.89 million people would have their disability payments' removed, or modified, under plans to abolish Personal Independent Payments (Pip) for working age people.

The party would also remove the extra health-related payments on Universal Credit.

A new system, called a Health Security Allowance, would replace both Pip and the Universal Credit health element but only the most "severe, enduring and high-risk cases" would receive cash support, the document says.

Other claimants would be supported through a council-run programme to cover what Reform said would be the "verifiable additional costs" as a result of their disability.

To boost available support for people out of work, the party says it would spend an extra Â£1.85bn a year on interventions such as cognitive behavioural therapy, physiotherapy, and employment support.

Reform also wants to reform children's benefits, and is promising to align the system for anxiety, depression and ADHD in young people with its changes to the adult system. But this would only apply to new claimants.

News.title: Ariana Grande leaves problems at home as her tour hits the UK
News.content:
It feels inconsiderate of Ariana Grande to bring a tour called Eternal Sunshine to the UK at the tail end of the year's fifth heatwave. Haven't we suffered enough already?

But the fans packed into London's O2 arena on Saturday night didn't seem to care about the heat and the sweat.

They came ready to dance. Thousands of them, dressed in cat ears, bridal gowns and elaborate floral headpieces.

They scream when she references rumours she's back together with her ex, Ricky Alvarez. And they bounce in unison when she plays colourful club anthems like Into You and Break Free.

It's the first time Grande has played in the UK since 2019, partly because of Covid, but also because of her Oscar-nominated role in the movie musical Wicked.

She rewards fans with a few of Glinda's signature hair tosses, external and, more importantly, a two-hour show that highlights the incredible agility of the star's voice.

Sure, the production has all the paraphernalia a major pop tour - big sets, plumes of smoke, inspired choreography - but there are long stretches where it's just Grande on stage with her band. Her stunning, four octave vocals come first. Everything else is a distant second. And rightly so.

If you dig around on Grande's YouTube channel, there's a famous video of her recording the song Positions, external, directing her sound engineers as she layers vocal harmonies and ad libs, finding new note combinations on the fly.

It's a bravura performance that showcases her facility with melody and arrangement - and she essentially recreates it live on stage at the O2.

After the opening run of songs, she hushes the audience and spends two minutes looping her voice. First the lyric, "I don't care what people say, it's true", in high and low registers. Then she adds short phrases: "Won't break. Can't Shake. Deep breathsâ¦. Tight chest. Life. Death. Rewind."

They become the backbone of the next song, Eternal Sunshine.

They're also the backstory of the whole show.

News.title: What's driving men to get penis fillers, despite the risks?
News.content:
Jason didn't want a "Coke can" â that's the nickname for a penis that has been enlarged with so much filler it resembles a stubby drink can.

"Some people go really overboard," Jason tells me when we meet in Manchester.

His procedure increased the girth of his penis by 16% - an amount he, and his partner, are really happy with. He says it has given him a "self-confidence boost".

"Everything still functions" as normal, Jason explains - just with "that extra little bit of width".

It is not clear how many men like Jason are having penis fillers. And you can't walk down the street and get a sense of it in the way you can visibly see the popularity of lip fillers. There is little regulation and there are no official records as anybody can start offering the procedure.

Penis fillers even became the topic of a bizarre conspiracy theory at the last Winter Olympics. Male ski jumpers were rumoured to be using fillers to increase the surface area of their suits so they could jump further.

However, some men have ended up in A&E with a penis turning black and skin "sloughing off" after a botched procedure. And the British Association of Urological Surgeons has issued warnings to men having these procedures.

So why are men doing it and what are the risks?

News.title: Friends, finances and finding your feet - advice for this year's freshers
News.content:
Journalism student Kieran Miller was worried about money, but he compared student bank accounts and chose one that gave him a free 16-25 Railcard, and signed up for student discount schemes.

Though it might be exciting to see your first maintenance loan payment hit your bank account in one big lump sum, Kieran, 19, says you need to remember it has to last until the next instalment.

With the help of his mum, Kieran, from Swansea, made a provisional budget before moving away, but warns that it's easy to get caught up in the student experience and spend more than you planned to.

"When you start uni and you're living away from your family and you've got this new sense of freedom it was also really difficult to stay strict financially because you want to make mates with people," he says. "Someone might invite you to go for food or to go for a drink - and you're like, 'I don't really want to say no because this is a chance to connect with someone.'"

As well as student loans, most universities offer a variety of scholarships and bursaries, and it's worth checking whether you're eligible.

News.title: The influencers getting bitten while chasing the perfect shark shot
News.content:
Incidents of sharks biting humans are incredibly rare, but at least three influencers have been bitten by the animals in less than a year. Scientists say they're increasingly concerned about the rise in social media videos showing people swimming too close to sharks, touching or even riding them.

"I'm seeing these videos every single week now and it's way more than it ever used to be," says shark scientist Kristian Parton, who also hosts the 'Shark Bytes' YouTube channel. "We're going to see people ending up in really serious incidents with sharks."

In July, a fishing influencer almost lost his leg after being attacked by a reef shark whilst spearfishing. In December, a Chinese content creator was bitten in the Maldives. Both incidents were caught on camera.

Researchers at the International Shark Attack File, which tracks human-shark interactions worldwide, have also told the BBC they've seen a marked increase in the past three years of people being bitten while trying to take footage with sharks.

A recent study of "swim with wildlife" expeditions, external found influencers and photographers were the most likely to ignore safety instructions.

In February last year, a tourist in the Caribbean had both hands bitten off while trying to get a photograph of a bull shark from the shallows, according to local authorities. Two months later, a snorkeller in Israel carrying a "selfie stick" was killed by sharks, reportedly while trying to get photographs.

The risk of being bitten by a shark remains extremely low: the number of unprovoked shark attacks worldwide has remained broadly stable for the past 30 years, at about 70 bites per year.

While Tayane Dalazen was bitten by a nurse shark - known as a more docile species - some influencers have been filmed touching tiger sharks and even great whites.

"We're talking about a true apex predator, a very large wild animal," says Parton. "You wouldn't walk into the Serengeti and try and put your hand on the face of a lion."

Sharks will often use defensive or "exploratory" bites when presented by an unwelcome human in their personal space, he adds.

Human interactions can also cause stress to the animals. Scientific studies have shown that approaching or touching a shark leads to high levels of hormones called glucocorticoids. These can lead to a weakened immune system, increased mortality and aborted offspring.

"If you're approaching the shark and stressing it out, whether it be in a nursery habitat, a breeding ground, or a feeding area, you're depriving that shark of an area that's important to it to survive," explains Parton, "and that's definitely a problem."

One of the best-known shark content creators is Ocean Ramsey, a 38-year-old former model who shot to fame in 2019 after she was pictured swimming with one of the largest great white sharks ever seen.

News.title: UK-made drones strike targets inside Russia
News.content:
British-made drones are being used to strike targets in Russia for the first time.

The drones, built by two separate British companies, have been used in mainland Russia in widespread and successful targeting of military and industrial targets, including refineries and warehouses of online retailer Wildberries.

The strikes, first reported by the Sunday Times, external, are said to have caused more than Â£35bn in economic damage. A well-placed military source confirmed to the BBC the UK drones had been used.

British manufactured Storm Shadow missiles had earlier been used in the conflict, although this new phase is having a far more decisive impact.

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has previously said drones using UK components and configurations have been used to attack Russian territory, including a fuel depot in the Kamensky District of the Rostov Region.

In April, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) announced it would supply Ukraine tens of thousands of drones, including long-range strike devices, in its biggest ever package.

The MoD said its support for Ukraine is "unwavering" and would stand by its ally "until it wins".

A spokesperson said: "We are committed to providing the equipment Ukraine needs to defend itself against Putin's illegal invasion.

"This includes over 150,000 drones this year, cutting-edge Stone Cloak devices that hinder Russian air defences and innovative low-cost cruise missiles."

On Sunday, Moscow's mayor said about 600 Ukrainian drones were launched towards the city overnight, with roughly a third of the drones being destroyed, and three people were injured.

A warehouse belonging to Russian online retailer Wildberries was hit.

Wildberries, known as Russia's version of Amazon, has been repeatedly targeted since July.

Kyiv said at the time it was targeting logistics hubs used by Russians to buy military equipment and disrupting supplies to the Russian army.

News.title: Athletics medal ceremonies postponed after fraud arrest
News.content:
Medal ceremonies at the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham were postponed after a man was arrested on suspicion of fraud.

West Midlands Police said concerns were raised after a man was found in an area of Alexander Stadium on Saturday evening without the right accreditation.

Transport at the tournament was suspended as a result of the arrest and necessary security procedures.

Members of the crowd reported being held outside by security staff for more than an hour after the event finished, with a large police presence at the scene.

The evening session concluded with Great Britain winning a pair of gold medals in the men's and women's 4x100m relays.

Tournament organisers said transport was suspended while the necessary security measures took place, but operations had returned to normal in the early hours of Sunday.

A statement from Birmingham 2026 said: "The safety and wellbeing of our spectators, athletes, workforce and the wider Championships' family will always be our first priority.

"We recognise that the delays presented challenges for those affected and would like to thank everyone for their patience, understanding and cooperation throughout the evening."

More information relating to the postponed medal ceremonies is due to be released later.

A West Midlands Police spokesperson said a man in his 30s remained in custody for questioning.

The crowd at the Alexander Stadium appeared to be near its 23,000 capacity.

At one point during the session, there was an announcement that the six medal ceremonies, scheduled to take place after the final event between 22:00 and 23:00 BST were cancelled, understood to be in relation to the police incident.

People posted on social media, reporting "crazy queues" for the shuttle bus and blue flashing lights on the main road outside the stadium.

A statement on the event's official account, posted on X at 23:03, said: "We apologise for the significant delays in leaving the Alexander Stadium venue this evening.

"Buses and coaches will start to arrive and departures will begin to gradually take place.

"We thank you for your patience with this matter. Please listen to the instructions from the safety personnel and marshals who are there to support you."

News.title: 'Number of fatalities' and four injured after car drives on wrong side of motorway
News.content:
A number of people have died and four people have been taken to hospital following a two-vehicle crash in County Kildare.

The collision occurred on on the M9 Northbound at Junction 3 at about 03:00 local time on Sunday.

GardaÃ­ (Irish police) said a vehicle had been travelling on the wrong side of the carriageway when a head on collision occurred with a second car. They said there were a "number of fatalities".

The driver and front passenger, both female and aged in their 30s, of the second car have been removed from the scene to Tallaght University Hospital and both remain in critical condition.

A female rear seat passenger, aged in her 20s, was taken to St. Luke's General Hospital and is in a serious condition.

The third passenger, who is a child, has been removed to Children's Health Ireland at Crumlin and is in a serious condition.

The section of the M9 from Junction 3 to Junction 4 northbound and southbound remains closed with local diversions in place.

Irish broadcaster RTÃ have reported that gardaÃ­ said there was no pursuit taking place when the collision occurred.

GardaÃ­ said FiosrÃº (the Office of the Police Ombudsman) has been notified of the incident.

FiosrÃº's on-call team of investigators attended the scene and an independent investigation is ongoing.

The watchdog said a FiosrÃº investigation relates to incidents involving contact with gardaÃ­ where a member of the public has died or been seriously injured.

It said a referral does not necessarily mean a garda or gardaÃ­ have been accused of wrongdoing.

"Instead, it means that FiosrÃº should independently investigate the incident to ascertain whether or not the act or omission of a garda or gardaÃ­ may have resulted in the death of, or serious harm to, a person," it added.

News.title: Parents 'watering down baby milk' over high costs
News.content:
A baby bank says parents are turning to "unsafe" practices such as watering down baby formula milk to save money.

Megan Sinden, founder of Moorside Baby Bank in Consett, County Durham, said a couple of families spoke of putting less powder in to get another week's worth out of it, "which to me is quite dangerous".

She called for a cap on rising costs of formula, saying: "It's not a luxury item, it's a basic need for a baby."

Charity National Childbirth Trust (NCT) said its recent study found nearly half of parents (48%) were struggling more financially after having a baby, and added infant formula should always be prepared according to the manufacturer's instructions.

Infant formula is designed to provide the correct balance of nutrients for babies when mothers cannot or choose not to breastfeed, and adding extra water alters that balance.

The lower concentration can cause nutrient deficiency, coupled with the reduced ability of the baby's body to absorb the nutrients, NCT said.

"In turn, this can lead to poor weight gain, growth problems, and developmental delays," the spokesperson said.

"In serious cases, too much water in the formula may lead to more immediate health problems because a baby's body is not able to safely process the excess water."

The latest report, external by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) found the average retail price of some infant formula had increased by more than 25% in recent years.

Moorside Baby Bank opened in February 2025 and has so far helped 226 families with goods like clothes, nappies and baby wipes, which were mainly donated by the community.

Sinden, who is a community worker from nearby Stanley, said the bank struggled to get donations of baby milk "because it is so expensive" and instead relied on grants to buy the formula in.

News.title: Unauthorised sites are growing but travellers say they are forced to break the law
News.content:
The number of unauthorised Gypsy and traveller sites is on the rise, with developments often carried out over Bank Holiday weekends.

Since April, sites in Hertfordshire, Essex, Cambridgeshire, Bedfordshire and elsewhere have been transformed, prompting legal battles and local dismay.

In January, the number of unauthorised traveller caravans â those without planning permission â across England stood at 4,950, a 73% increase on January 2020's figure of 2,860.

The summer count also shows a rise, of 44% between July 2019 and July 2025, from 3,113 to 4,471.

A senior councillor in one affected area warns there has been a "loss of control" of the planning system, while villagers living near one site likened its rapid construction to a "military operation".

The government says unauthorised development is "totally unacceptable" and that councils have "strong powers" to tackle it.

But Cliff Codona, who founded and chairs the National Travellers' Action Group, says the planning system is like a "big dagger in their back" for travellers, leaving them no option but to "break the law".

So what do travellers say is driving some to act unlawfully, and what do others think?

News.title: Britain's youngest Formula E driver says talent isn't enough anymore
News.content:
Making split-second decisions while driving up to 200mph probably seems like a crazy task for most of us.

But Britain's youngest Formula E driver is learning to take it in his stride as his second season in the series draws to a close.

Back in 2024, Taylor Barnard became the youngest person to start an E-Prix and since then he's broken several other records - including becoming the youngest driver to secure a podium, pole and points in the sport.

So what's the 22-year-old got his sights set on now? The ultimate title, of course, world champion.

Barnard tells BBC Newsbeat he feels he got into racing by the "skin of my teeth", due to the extreme costs it takes to climb the motorsport ladder.

The immense financial backing needed to become a professional driver has been long known, with stars like Sir Lewis Hamilton speaking openly about the sacrifices his family made to get him a seat in Formula 1.

And Barnard feels if he was trying to climb the ranks now, he wouldn't make it due to prices being "so blown out of proportion".

News.title: Soldiers praised for 'phenomenal job' helping crews tackle wildfires
News.content:
A chief fire officer has praised soldiers for supporting crews tackling wildfires in south Wales.

Fin Monahan said South Wales Fire and Rescue Service was under severe pressure and very grateful to seven other fire services and the military for help.

About 200 members of the Queen's Own Gurkha Logistic Regiment, with support from 22 Royal Engineers, Royal Logistics Corp and Army helicopters have been been involved.

Crews from London, Cumbria and elsewhere have also been providing support.

Monahan told the BBC the UK and Welsh governments took "a very serious step" in bringing in the military but the "extra capacity" was needed as crews fought dozens of fires across the country.

He said his firefighters have "very specialist skills" to tackle wildfires with military assistance enabling him to "focus all of that in the right place".

Soldiers have been providing logistical support, including water distribution, to assist firefighters and specialist responders.

Monahan described the soldiers as "doing an utterly phenomenal job digging trenches and also helping us build fire breaks".

"That has liberated lots of our firefighters to go and do their more specialist skills of firefighting."

News.title: Doctor tells inquiry hospital concerns ignored for 15 years
News.content:
A doctor involved in the development of Scotland's super-hospital has claimed his concerns over patient safety were repeatedly ignored.

Dr Michael Bradnam told the Scottish Hospitals Inquiry he had spent 15 years raising issues with ventilation systems, electrical safety and humidity control at the Queen Elizabeth University Hospital (QEUH) campus in Glasgow.

In a late submission to the probe, launched in the wake of a series of patient deaths, Bradnam said there had been no "formal responses" to his complaints.

NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde (NHSGGC) said it was reviewing the evidence, but that patient safety remained its "utmost concern".

The inquiry was launched in 2019 to examine mistakes made in the planning, design and construction of the QEUH campus, which includes the Royal Hospital for Children (RHC), following concerns about unusual infections and the deaths of four patients.

Scotland's independent public prosecution and death investigation authority is looking into seven deaths for potential links to the environment at the hospital.

News.title: Walk-outs, infighting and a failed budget: The first 100 days of a Plaid Cymru and Reform-led Wales
News.content:

Wales knew a political earthquake was coming, but when it struck, in May this year, the country’s 3 million residents were still left reeling by the result.

Labour was dealt an astounding defeat in the Welsh election, losing their grip on the Senedd for the first time in 26 years. With the party reduced to just nine Members of the Senedd (MS), the chamber has gone from being overwhelmingly Labour red to a mix of the green of Plaid Cymru and the light blue of Reform UK.

Welsh nationalists Plaid Cymru and their leader Rhun ap Iorwerth have established a minority government, with Nigel Farage’s “insurgent” party holding a third of the chamber, in what is their strongest foothold in regional politics.

But these two parties are not natural bedfellows, and there have been explosive rows, walkouts and even tears in the first 100 days of this new-look Welsh government.

Plaid are proud champions of the Nation of Sanctuary scheme for refugees, hope to invest more in social care and push for greater devolved powers – with the eventual goal of an independence referendum. Meanwhile, Reform are staunchly anti-immigration, wish to slash public spending and firmly believe in remaining part of the UK.

Describing the last three months as a “pretty wild ride”, Reform MS for Caerdydd Penarth Joe Martin said his party has “definitely made our mark” in forming the main opposition.

open image in gallery Reform's leader Dan Thomas is a newcomer to Welsh politics ( Getty )

“Plaid Cymru have a lot of crazy, radical ideas and it’s our job to oppose this,” he said. “The example of this would be their push for independence. Our position has been really clear on devolution – we want to see Plaid doing a good job with the devolved powers they already have.”

In June, Mr Martin was at the centre of a controversial debate over Wales’ “pointless” international spending, and the rate of illiteracy in the “underfunded” Welsh education system. During one exchange, he joked that he had tried to ask Welsh students for their opinion, but had received no response given that they could not read.

As a result, members of Plaid Cymru, Labour and the Green Party walked out in protest. He has also been rebuked by the presiding officer of the Senedd after a speech in which he claimed attacks from Sudanese asylum seekers were “inevitable”, which left one Labour MS struggling to hold back tears.

Asked about Reform’s unabashed approach to the debating chamber, Mr Martin said: “The support for what I’ve said has been overwhelming, and that shows that there has been a massive demand for a new party to say what the average person is thinking.

“I stand by the way I said it, but I think ridiculous ideas need to be ridiculed.”

Reform is now chairing five out of the 13 Senedd committees, including the climate change, environment, sustainability and rural affairs committee. Its chair, James Evans, is a Conservative Party defector who has previously said that rural Wales is “under attack” from green energy infrastructure, and that Reform would ban new onshore wind farms.

open image in gallery Plaid Cymru are pushing for greater devolved powers - while Reform are staunchly pro-union ( AFP/Getty )

Mr Farage and his closest allies are also long-term climate-change sceptics, and have previously pledged to scrap net zero and have described its policies as “lunacy”.

Professor Laura McAllister, a professor of public policy and governance of Wales, said: “It’s hard at this stage to gauge the approach Reform Party chairs will take in each of those committees.

“What will likely happen, and this is very much an observation on how politics has worked since May, is that we see in Reform exactly what they are – an insurgent movement that is trying to translate itself into a party.”

She added that they had an “eclectic group” of 34 MSs, with the majority sharing no previous experience of politics, although Mr Martin points out that many have arrived with years of experience in the private sector.

While they have been successful in gaining cross-party support in motions such as tackling bovine TB and calling for a statutory register of lobbyists, other headlines have suggested an element of confusion within the party. In June, 11 Reform MSs voted to effectively criticise their own party, when Plaid Cymru tabled a motion to say that they had no commitments to tackling childcare.

open image in gallery Reform UK leader Nigel Farage (left) and Reform UK leader in Wales Dan Thomas at the Reform UK manifesto launch for the Senedd elections in May (Ben Birchall/PA) ( PA Wire )

The selection of their leader Dan Thomas also attracted controversy. A former London council leader who twice stood as a Conservative parliamentary candidate, Mr Thomas only entered frontline Welsh politics three months before the election after he was personally selected by Mr Farage.

Despite winning the election, it has not all been smooth sailing for Plaid Cymru either, with their supplementary budget failing to pass in July before the summer recess.

A row with Labour emerged over funding plans for the education of children with additional learning needs, with Plaid failing to secure enough support to pass their spending plans.

Plaid’s finance minister Elin Jones said she was “flabbergasted” at Labour’s stance, and accused the party of behaving as a “destructive opposition”.

Professor McAllister said: “The supplementary budget is less significant, although it is symbolic that it wasn’t able to pass because it’s the first time it has happened.

“Ahead of an autumn/winter budget, Plaid needs to be much clearer about where its concessions are coming from.

“They need to be more strategic about that to avoid a standoff in a budget debate, because that would be a disastrous look. It’s about the actual constitutional implications. If a budget can’t be passed then a further general election has to be forced.”

Mr ap Iorwerth had campaigned with a 100-day plan, which would see restrictions announced on smartphone use in schools, strategic reviews across public services, cutting waiting lists and ambitious childcare plans.

In September, he will be under pressure to deliver. After nearly three decades of Labour, with a struggling economy and the worst poverty, health and education standards in the country, the Welsh public made clear in the election that change is needed – and fast.

Ukrainian forces have used British drones to attack deep inside Russia’s mainland for the first time, according to a report.

In an indication of strengthening military ties between the UK and Kyiv, Ukrainian army sources told The Times that drones made by two British companies have been used in the past six months to attack targets including oil refineries in Volgograd and near Moscow and logistics hubs.

The intensifying drone attacks, which have also targeted transport infrastructure and sites belonging to Russia’s largest online retailer, Wildberries, have been crucial in inflicting heavy damage on Moscow’s economy.

open image in gallery British drones have been used in deepening attacks inside Russia ( AFP/Getty )

The revelations will further harm the relationship between the UK and Moscow, with tensions increasing over the presence of Russian vessels near UK waters, and the chief of defence staff declaring that the UK is facing the highest level of threat from Russia since the Cold War.

“Russia has been very effective at keeping the West nervous about hitting it too hard. These attacks mean the UK is effectively signalling to Russia and our allies that we’re not [nervous] any more,” one defence source told the newspaper.

The Wiltshire-built Nyan drone, developed by BAE Systems subsidiary Callen-Lenz and tested by the Royal Navy, was used to strike Belgorod near the Russian border, the report said.

First tested by BAE Systems this summer, the drone has a wingspan of 2.9 metres and can fly more than 150 miles, the defence company said on its website.

“We deliver a range of capabilities into the UK MoD as part of the UK’s support to the defence of Ukraine,” the company confirmed to The Times. “The Nyan uncrewed air system provides a rapidly developed platform proven in meeting emerging threats within highly contested environments.”

open image in gallery Former prime minister Keir Starmer looks at drones as he visits defence contractor Stark in Swindon in June ( AFP/Getty )

The second drone used by the Ukrainian military and made in British factories has a range of more than 600 miles. It is launched using a catapult system allowing drones to be fired in quick succession, according to The Times, which did not name the company for security reasons.

Ukraine’s long-range drone warfare has transformed the war. On Sunday, Kyiv attacked what was reportedly Russia’s largest Wildberries site, situated near Moscow, in a huge overnight air attack that included more than 800 drones, according to Moscow.

While the UK has provided Kyiv with Storm Shadow missiles, the supply is finite, and their range is only around 155 miles.

Earlier in the year, former chancellor Rachel Reeves confirmed a £752m payment to Ukraine, part of a larger £3.36bn loan, which was earmarked to procure essential military equipment, including long-range missiles, advanced air defence systems, and drones.

Last year, it emerged that British parts had also been found in Russian drones.

Volodymyr Zelensky said microcomputers for flight control, manufactured in the UK, were discovered in drones involved in a deadly assault. Other parts from allied countries, including the US, were also identified.

He called for more stringent sanctions against British companies implicated in supplying components for Russian drones.

Gurkhas have been deployed to South Wales to help tackle wildfires as the much of the country remains in tinderbox conditions.

South Wales Fire and Rescue Service (SWFRS) said on Sunday it was responding to “significant wildfire activity” with the support of other services from across the UK and military personnel.

As SWFRS crews tackled ten large fires across the region on Saturday, around 100 personnel, including members of the Queen's Own Gurkha Logistic Regiment (QOGLR) and 22 royal engineers, were deployed for logistical, operational and planning support.

A further 100 are expected to follow, the Ministry of Defence said on Saturday.

open image in gallery Nepalese Gurkhas have worked alongside the British Army as part of a 200-year tradition ( UK MOD Crown copyright )

The QOGLR is a unit of the Royal Logistic Corps composed of Nepalese Gurkhas and British officers, a symbol of the 200-year military tradition that has seen Nepal’s soldiers fight alongside the British Army.

The special forces helped with water distribution and logistical support so firefighters and specialist responders could focus on frontline firefighting.

Water was transported by military personnel from distant sources to create a mobile water reservoir in key locations, the Ministry of Defence said. They also helped move equipment, supplies and personnel to ensure resources reached critical locations quickly.

Military teams also helped emergency services access remote and difficult terrain, improving their ability to respond to the ongoing fires

open image in gallery Gurkha’s helped create a mobile water reservoir in key locations ( UK MOD Crown copyright )

The risk of wildfires in South Wales remains high due to a lack of rain, despite temperatures easing in the coming days.

Firefighters have been working 10 or 11-hour shifts on mountainsides without breaks or access to toilets, eating meals “covered in soot”, Gareth Tovey, Fire Brigades Union executive council member for Wales said.

Deputy chief fire officer Adam Openshaw said: “The combined efforts of everyone involved in this major incident continue to play a vital role in keeping people safe during these exceptional circumstances.

“We know this is a challenging and worrying time for many people.

“Please be assured that we remain committed to protecting our communities and keeping the people of South Wales safe.”

On Friday evening, millions of people in England and Wales received an alert on their mobile devices warning them of a “very high risk of wildfires nationally”.

It came after Prime Minister Andy Burnham described Britain as a “tinderbox” and a temporary ban on disposable barbecues was put in place.

SWFRS said on Saturday evening that it had already received 736 calls, compared with an average of about 300, and urged people only to call 999 if there was a new emergency to report.

Anthony Hopkins has revealed the moment he decided to seek help for alcohol addiction, after realising he “could have taken out a whole family” while driving drunk.

The 88-year-old Welsh superstar – who has won two Oscars, for his performances in The Silence of the Lambs and The Father – has been open about addiction and the effect it had on his early career and those closest to him. In a new interview, he went into detail about the turning point that convinced him to turn his life around.

“I go back to 1975, 27 December,” he told The Observer. “I was driving my car, going to a party. I was in an alcoholic blackout. I knew about alcoholism but I didn’t want to confront it. I realised I could have taken out a whole family by my driving. And someone in New York had said: ‘If you ever want to talk to anyone … phone this number.’ And on the Monday morning, I phoned the number. And it was AA. I said: ‘I’ll come and see you.’ I didn’t want anyone coming to me. I still had some sort of pride.”

He continued: “An elderly lady was there, was very kind. She said: ‘How do you feel?’, and I said: ‘I know I’m in big trouble and I don’t know what to do.’ She said: ‘Well, you don’t ever have to drink again.’ And she said – I knew she was going to do it – ‘Why don’t you just trust in God?’ And I got down on the street, and an immensely powerful voice inside me said: ‘Now it’s all over. You can start living … and it has all been for a purpose.’ And that craving for drink left me. It’s never come back. In 50 years.”

open image in gallery Anthony Hopkins in 2019 ( AFP/Getty )

Hopkins previously wrote about his addiction to alcohol in his memoir We Did OK, Kid, which was released last year. In it, he described booze making him pick fights with directors and collaborators, and that it made him a poor husband to his first two wives. “That’s the ugly side of alcoholism,” he wrote. “It brought out a brutal side of me. I’m not proud of it at all.”

He also recalled making a “terrible early 1970s film” that he has no recollection of appearing in. “No one in that movie could remember a minute of doing it: we’d all been blackout drunk,” he wrote.

Hopkins is currently promoting his debut album, Life Is a Dream, which is inspired by his memories of growing up in Margam, south Wales, and the farmland, meadows and mountains that surrounded his family home in the 1940s. The album comprises of songs Hopkins has written over the last six decades, but never published until now.

open image in gallery Anthony Hopkins recording his new album in the studio ( PA )

While Hopkins began acting almost 70 years ago and has won numerous awards including four Baftas, he said in a statement that music was actually his “first desire”.

“I’ve been composing music all my life,” he said. “Some of these pieces have lived with me for decades and I still find myself returning to them.”

Hopkins is considered one of the world’s greatest living actors, with credits that range from the period drama The Remains of the Day to David Lynch’s The Elephant Man and several of the movies in the Thor franchise. He has played cannibal serial killer Hannibal Lecter in three films, first in 1991’s The Silence of the Lambs, its sequel Hannibal (2001) and is prequel Red Dragon (2002).

If you or someone you know is suffering from alcohol addiction, you can confidentially call the national alcohol helpline Drinkline on 0300 123 1110 or visit the NHS website here for information about the programmes available to you.

Even after a night of heavy bombardment, Olga wakes up at dawn and gets ready to feed Odesa’s cats.

“This city is my whole life,” the 74-year-old tells The Independent. Each day, she tends to the 50 cats that roam the debris and burnt-out buildings in her neighbourhood, a consistent target of Vladimir Putin’s bombs.

Olga’s husband and son have both been dead for some time now, yet she doesn’t feel lonely – and she says she has long stopped panicking when air raid sirens go off.

“People are evacuating on their own, but I haven’t looked into doing that.”

Olga is among a group of elderly people left to look after abandoned pets and community strays. Even before the war, Ukraine had a large stray animal population – estimates put the number of dogs at up to 200,000 and many more stray cats – roaming the streets, according to the Naturewatch Foundation. Since the start of the war, thousands more pet dogs and cats have been lost or abandoned.

Experts have told The Independent that people who stay in their war-torn towns and cities often end up feeding dozens of animals despite having very limited resources of their own.

open image in gallery Olga is one of many elderly people looking after pets and strays ( United for Animals )

The work begins at 9am: “I go out to feed them. I start from the furthest points and end by the sea,” she says. Olga feeds the cats in her yard, neighbouring gardens, parking lots, and on the slopes along the way to the sea.

“Since childhood, I have loved cats very much,” she says.

Her favourite cat Lora, who she has nicknamed Chernushka, survived a tumour on the neck the size of a walnut. Since then, Olga has become very attached.

”She loves pâté and the tastiest food I can give her because she went through many surgeries. I had to nurse her back to health for a long time, so she became like a sick child – the most precious one.”

It is this love of animals that has stopped her from leaving Odesa despite the dangers; her biggest fear is not for her own safety – it’s leaving the animals defenceless.

“They simply won’t survive without us humans,” she says.

open image in gallery Odesa has been under intensified strikes from Russia ( Reuters )

While not on the frontline, Odesa has been targeted by Russia with intensified strikes in an attempt to strangle Ukraine’s commercial links with the outside world. Attacks have taken place along the coastline, targeting vessels and port infrastructure while Moscow tries to protect its own ships through the Azov-Black Sea basin.

On the other side of the city and totally unbeknownst to Olga, 73-year-old Nataliia remains a devoted carer to 13 pets and 27 strays.

“Living in a war zone is very difficult. The war has a very negative effect on my health and the state of my animals; they become nervous. I have to spend a lot of time monitoring their wellbeing and calming them,” she says.

“It’s very hard to live without electricity and water, and sometimes even without heat during the cold season. Carrying water up to the eighth floor for the stray animals is tough – when the water in their bowls freezes, I have to thaw it and bring out hot water. All of this significantly complicates living conditions.”

Food for the animals comes out of her pension, with the United for Animals Foundation charity helping provide food for the strays.

open image in gallery Nataliia spends her pension money on food for the animals ( United for Animals )

“We are helping hundreds – dozens of hundreds – of stray animals survive. Animals that live in conditions of cold, hunger, constant explosions, and fear, when they are afraid to even come out of their shelters.”

Getting pet food and supplies to these caregivers can be a challenge as many of the elderly recipients can’t carry the heavy bags from collection points, according to Martyna Maciejewska, the senior manager of field operations for Greater Good Charities.

“Reaching communities closer to the frontlines is even more difficult and dangerous,” she says. “Many elderly people have chosen to remain in their homes despite the conflict and continue caring for both their own pets and abandoned or community animals. Delivering supplies to these areas often requires navigating active security risks, making every delivery more complex and hazardous.

“The need has remained consistently high throughout the war. Many elderly caregivers survive on pensions of only 2,500–4,500 UAH [approximately £40-75] per month, making it extremely difficult to cover utilities, their own basic needs, and the cost of feeding animals. Without outside support, many would simply be unable to continue caring for the pets and strays that depend on them.”

Nataliia’s day starts at 6am and ends at 1am, as she cleans numerous litter boxes, feeds them and checks all the animals are healthy and uninjured after a night of air raids.

“During explosions, I worry deeply about the lives of both my pets and the street animals – especially the ones on the street, who could be hit by shrapnel or caught in a blast.”

“Since the war began, the animals’ behaviour has changed significantly. First, they have become more demanding about food and require more of it. Second, they have become more fearful. If shelling starts, they scatter, and it is then very difficult to gather them all back to their feeding area. My animals are my life; we are one whole.”

open image in gallery The number of stray animals in Ukraine has risen during the conflict ( AFP/Getty )

Scientists have found that animals’ behaviour had significantly changed due to the war. Researchers in Ukraine compared the impact of conflict on wildlife by observing their behaviour after the Russian occupation with the same period in 2021. In a study published in June, they concluded that conflict significantly altered animals’ daily patterns. They became less active during the night or when active conflict was ongoing.

Olga has seen the animals change too, proposing that human nature has had just a significant impact on the animals’ behaviour as the shelling.

“What causes the most discomfort is that some people are against feeding animals... specifically near cars. A car is worth more than an animal to them. Of course, there are scandals and a lot of stress. My heart aches because of this, and my blood pressure rises, because not everyone treats animals with understanding.

“They suffer most from cruel people.”

Despite having seen the cruelty of conflict towards animals, both Nataliia and Olga have hope that the war will end soon.

“Hope is all that’s left. Because there is no end or edge in sight, and the forecasts here are not very comforting,” Olga says.

Nataliia adds: “I truly hope it ends soon. I hope Ukrainian men return to their families soon, that children and women stop crying, and that mothers stop crying at their sons’ funerals.”
