Reform UK has set out plans to revolutionise the welfare state that would see almost three million people’s disability and sickness payments withdrawn or modified.

Under the plans, Reform would abolish personal independence payments (Pip) and the health element of Universal credit for working-age adults, The Telegraph reports. Reform’s Treasury spokesperson Robert Jenrick claimed that the proposals would cut £50 billion from the welfare bill.

He said that Reform would introduce a new, regularly-reviewed, health security allowance that would provide support only for the “gravely ill and severely challenged”.

Labour said the £50 billion claim was “fantasy economics” and said stripping people of benefit payments would shift costs onto employers.

Mr Jenrick said 6.9 million people were receiving disability benefits but “this is not an epidemic of broken backs and lost limbs” as since 2002 the share of working-age people claiming for mental health and behavioural conditions had tripled.

Under the planned reforms, due to be unveiled in detail on Monday, cash payments for low-level conditions would end and be replaced with disability support accounts, run by local councils and mayors, to cover costs such as equipment, adaptations, transport and personal assistance.

And employers could be obliged to pay a “return to work cover” insurance to fund the cost of the first two years after an employee is signed off sick.

Mr Jenrick said firms would then have a “strong economic incentive” to return the employee to work. People who had not returned to work within two years would go through a single, rigorous assessment conducted in person to “screen out vexatious and fraudulent claims”.

open image in gallery Robert Jenrick said ‘dumping our young people onto welfare isn’t compassion’ ( PA )

Writing in The Telegraph, Mr Jenrick said: “We will not pretend this is painless.

“Existing claimants will be reassessed over three to four years: we estimate that 2.16 million will keep their present cash entitlement in full, while 2.89 million will see theirs modified or withdrawn, concentrated where recent growth has been most explosive.”

He said the state must be there to support people who need it but “dumping our young people onto welfare isn’t compassion; it’s neglect”.

“We are not lifting people out of misfortune. We are abandoning them to it, and calling it kindness.”

Mr Jenrick said the Reform proposals would save “more than double” the £23 billion promised by Kemi Badenoch’s Conservatives, with £22 billion of the savings coming from changes to disability benefits alone.

open image in gallery Helen Whately, Shadow Secretary of State for Work and Pensions ( Getty )

Abdi Mohamed, head of policy at disability equality charity Scope, said the party’s proposals “should be about creating opportunities, not pushing disabled people into poverty and calling it compassion.

“Life costs a huge amount more when you’re disabled, and PIP goes towards covering those costs, whether or not you're in work. It's not an unemployment benefit.”

He added: “Young disabled people are facing a multitude of barriers getting into work, but slashing billions in financial support for disabled people won’t fix that. We need to be far more ambitious about tackling inaccessible workplaces, improving employment support, and ensuring employers provide the adjustments disabled people need to work.”

Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said the plans were an attempt to distract attention from the investigation into a £5 million donation to Nigel Farage and his “pointless by-election” in Clacton.

She said: “Reform have been nowhere on the debate on welfare reform. They have flip-flopped on restoring the two child benefit cap and claimed they’ll only take benefits away from foreigners, which won’t do enough to bring down the overall bill.

“The Conservatives are on the side of working people and we’re clear about our plans. Restore the two-child benefit cap, end benefits for low level mental health conditions, remove benefits from foreign nationals and restore face-to-face assessments.”

A Labour spokeswoman said: “Reform’s £50 billion claim is fantasy economics, built on stripping support from disabled people and shifting costs onto employers.”

She added that the Labour Government’s reforms to welfare “deliver credible, independently-costed savings, not arbitrary numbers with no credible plan behind them”.

News.title: Rashford returns and Fernandes misses another penalty as Man Utd humbled by Amorim
News.content:
Manchester United 2 AC Milan 4

Bruno Fernandes missed a penalty for the second successive pre-season friendly as Manchester United were beaten 4-2 by former head coach Ruben Amorim’s AC Milan.

Fernandes, who rolled a spot-kick wide in a shoot-out against Leeds in midweek, was gifted the chance to open his pre-season account in Wroclaw, Poland.

His effort was on target this time, but Milan keeper Lorenzo Torriani dived to his right to beat the shot away.

Fernandes did at least get an assist, taking the second-minute corner which was powerfully headed home by Harry Maguire to give United the lead.

News.title: Newcastle kit fiasco sums up haphazard pre-season
News.content:
Newcastle United 1 Bayer Leverkusen 2

Newcastle’s pre-season friendly against Bayer Leverkusen at St James’ Park took a bizarre turn when a kit clash prompted the hosts to change shirts midway through the first half.

The German team’s white away kit with blue trim proved hard to distinguish from Newcastle’s home strip, which has a white back and blue stripes across the shoulders.

During the first-half hydration break, Newcastle decided to change into their lilac third kit, which improved the viewing experience for fans who took to social media to question the original choice of kits.

Newcastle would go on to lose the game 2-1 in new manager Matthias Jaissle’s first game at St James’, a result which followed a 3-1 reverse against Everton on Wednesday evening.

Leverkusen, the 2023-24 Bundesliga champions now managed by Spaniard Carles Martínez Novell, scored after just 44 seconds through a powerful Ibrahim Maza strike.

News.title: Raul Jimenez’s late penalty seals share of spoils for Wolves against Blackburn
News.content:
Cesar Peixoto wants Wolves to play with their heads rather than their hearts after the home side rescued a late point in the first game of the Championship season following relegation. Wolves replaced Rob Edwards with Portuguese coach Peixoto during the summer and he felt his side’s loss of organisation allowed Blackburn to take control of the game.

Peixoto said: “One point is not what we want, we want three points. We lost some organisation in the second half and played more with our hearts and not our heads and brains.

“We have to keep our mental stability during the 90 minutes because we’re better when we’re organised. We need to play our way with our identity. It’s a lesson for us to understand when we lose organisation it’s more difficult for us and more easy for the opposition.

“We’re working hard to bring more solutions [into the club] but we need to work hard with the players we have. It’s the first game, there’s a lot to work on and a lot to improve.”

Mowbray: It feels like a defeat

Tony Mowbray took charge of Blackburn in the league for the first time since returning to the club for a second stint in the dugout. Rovers recorded their lowest league finish since Mowbray’s first stint in charge of the club last term but the Blackburn boss is confident his side have enough to beat the drop and climb up the table this campaign.

Mowbray said: “Ultimately, it feels like a defeat, it’s a bit disappointing and a bit frustrating. I just felt a lot of decisions were starting to swing their way. It’s harsh to take, I don’t think they deserved a second goal. We asked the players to be brave and we were collectively very strong.

“Everybody has us relegated, probably on the back of finishing 20th last season and losing a couple of our better players and not spending much money, which is a good motivation for the team. We deserved to win the game, we showed there’s enough quality to give teams problems and I hope there’s help on the way [in the transfer window].”

The first chance of the season came the way of Blackburn as a cross-field pass found Alebiosu down the right, who floated a ball into the box only for an unmarked Oladipo Afolayan to head wide from eight-yards out.

However, Wolves scored the first goal of the new campaign when Fer Lopez played a defence-splitting through ball into the path of Munetsi, who coolly found the net with a first time effort from the edge of the penalty area.

News.title: How to have the perfect slow-paced holiday in Zakynthos
News.content:
Zakynthos, also known as Zante, is renowned for raucous nightlife, but there’s a far more authentic side to the Venetians “Fiore di Levante” (Flower of the East). For such a small island, scenery is extremely varied: the southern coastline – home to Laganas’ notorious nightlife strip – also encompasses the pristine beaches of Zakynthos Marine Park, where loggerhead sea turtles come to nest, while some of the island’s best-known attractions, including Navagio Beach on the cliff-lined northerly coast, can only be reached by boat.

Birthplace of the man who penned Greece’s national anthem, Zakynthos was also a magnet for literary greats: Byron lay in state here and philhellene Edgar Allan Poe wrote a sonnet to the island’s “verdant slopes”.

Last but not least, food is a powerful lure here: sit in a rustic sea view tavern sipping local Verdea white wine with a plate full of traditional kouneli stifado – a garlic and tomato-soaked rabbit stew – and you’ll be hooked.

News.title: Ebola doctors ‘step back’ from WHO in drug trial ethics row
News.content:
Two leading doctors have “stepped back” from long-held positions with the World Health Organization amid a row over the ethics of an Ebola drug trial underway in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The randomised control trial, called Ebo-Pep, is testing whether an experimental antiviral is an effective post-exposure treatment.

But experts believe the study’s design puts healthcare workers on the frontline of the epidemic at risk, because it means medics exposed to Ebola might receive a placebo treatment.

“We owe them [healthcare workers] a duty of care to do the best possible thing, and a 50 per cent chance of getting a placebo tablet is not that,” said Prof Tom Fletcher, director of the Global Health Trials Unit at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine. The WHO’s health emergencies clinical unit has also deployed him to Ebola ‘Red Zones’ for more than a decade.

This week, Prof Fletcher and eight other experts based in the UK, US, Uganda, Rwanda, Sierra Leone and Canada published their concerns in Nature Africa, calling for a “careful reconsideration” of the trial protocol.

They said they are not against Ebo-Pep or randomised trials, but warned there are “additional ethical obligations” when including healthcare workers in studies like this, given the case fatality rate currently stands at 40 per cent.

Prof Fletcher said: “Ebo-Pep is a really good trial, it’s the trial we’ve talked about doing for years. But we’re talking about [protecting] the ‘one-per-centers’, the people who willingly step into one of the most dangerous environments in the world.”

News.title: Wildfire watch: Inside London’s fire control centre on the hottest day of the year
News.content:
“It’s been relentless, an immense number of calls,” says Yvonne Woodhams, control room commander at the London Fire Brigade’s headquarters on the morning of what turned out to be the hottest day of the year so far.

Inside a nondescript building in South-west London, dozens of fire brigade dispatchers field calls from the public and direct the city’s 5,000 or so firefighters across 102 stations to where they are most needed.

In the middle of another heatwave and on a day when temperatures rose to just above 38 degrees, the control room was busy – the scale and frequency of wildfires in London’s parks and grasslands are now considered unprecedented.

Above the dispatchers there is a live map, with red dots representing each active fire, sprawling from Enfield in the north to Purley in the south.

Wildfires nearly always have a human origin like dropped cigarette butts, glass bottles that magnifies the sunlight, or the now-temporarily banned portable barbecues.

But it’s the tinderbox that London has become which is worrying firefighters.

Scorching hot, low-humidity weather, a bit of wind, and tinder-dry vegetation can cause the smallest spark to ignite an inferno. Conditions like this have been described as “fire weather” by the author John Vaillant.

News.title: Inside the biggest collection of venomous snakes in Latin America
News.content:
On the outskirts of São Paulo, several secure serpentariums sit in forested parkland. They contain some of the most venomous creatures on earth and provide the fuel for Latin America’s biggest antivenom manufacturing and research facility.

In one corner of the grounds, huts on stilts house five of Brazil’s most endangered snakes. One, the golden lancehead, is so rare that poachers asked $20,000 for a single specimen. It is found only on a tiny uninhabited island off the South Atlantic coast.

Nearby, inside the campus’s oldest building, a dip worn into the stone floor shows wear from the original serum-producing horses housed here over a century ago. Around it hang old scientific drawings and shelves stacked with journals bound in snakeskin.

Founded in 1901 by physician Dr Vital Brazil, the institute pioneered the development of species-specific antivenoms Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

This is Brazil’s Butantan Institute. Founded in 1901 to fight an outbreak of bubonic plague, it now produces almost all of the country's antivenoms, supplying at least 350,000 vials annually. It is part of a public health system that has made snakebite in Latin America far less deadly than almost anywhere else in the world.

Now, having spent over a century perfecting antivenom at home, Brazil is expanding its global impact – sharing not just its lifesaving sera, but its world-leading snake research.

Specimens in a jar at the institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

More than five million people are bitten by snakes around the world each year. Between 82,000 and 138,000 die, while roughly three times as many suffer amputations or permanent disability, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The burden falls heaviest on poor rural communities in Asia (up to two million bites annually) and Africa (around 500,000), where farmers, women and children walk through dense vegetation without protective clothing or access to nearby hospitals.

Across the Americas, the incidence of bites is far smaller. Some 57,000 are bitten by snakes each year, with Brazil accounting for over 30,000, according to the country’s health ministry.

But what stands out is the survival rate. According to the Pan American Health Organization (Paho), the region’s fatality rate is just 0.6 per cent – compared to up to 12 per cent in some rural regions of Africa.

Latin American snakes are no less dangerous. Venom from bothrops, a genus of the pit viper known locally as “jaracas”, can dissolve blood vessels, stop clotting and cause severe flesh rot or necrosis. Bites from the viper account for up to 90 per cent of reported envenomings each year in Brazil.

One of the snakes housed by the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s constitution legally obliges the state to provide treatment regardless of cost, resulting in antivenom having come to be seen as an essential public right, rather than a commodity for profit.

For poor rural workers who cannot afford treatment, receiving free antivenom quickly is what prevents a bite from becoming fatal.

Regional biology helps too. Unlike in Asia or Africa, where dozens of disparate snake families complicate treatment, the dominance of the Bothrops in Brazil makes life easier.

It means that rural clinics only need to stock a few versatile antivenoms rather than dozens of hyper-specialised ones. The Butantan Institute makes roughly 400,000 vials annually, more than enough to meet demand.

Yet even such a well-designed system struggles with the country’s unforgiving geography.

The Butantan Institute is home to Latin America’s largest collection of venomous species Credit : Camila Svenson

Covering nearly half of Brazil, the Amazon rainforest has vast roadless expanses where travel relies on slow wooden boats. For isolated communities, reaching a stocked clinic can take 12 to 24 hours – often beyond the critical window to prevent amputation or death.

Part of the challenge lies in the treatment itself. Traditional liquid antivenom must be administered intravenously under strict medical supervision due to the risk of acute allergic reactions. Crucially, it also requires an unbroken cold chain.

When exposed to tropical heat, the therapeutic proteins quickly denature and clump together. This renders the serum useless or, in the worst cases, dangerous.

Dr Grazziotin holds a tiny snake Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To overcome this, Brazil is increasingly deploying freeze-dried (lyophilised) antivenoms.

Though more expensive and complex to produce, these powder formulations withstand high heat and remain stable for years without cooling, needing only sterile water to reconstitute them for use.

The centuries-old process of creating antivenom is complex and relies on a method barely changed since its invention.

Reptiles at the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Pioneered in 1895 by French physician Albert Calmette in Saigon (now Ho Chi Minh), Vietnam, the process begins by manually milking live snakes for their venom.

Small, non-lethal doses are then injected into horses over several months, prompting their immune systems to produce high concentrations of specialised antibodies.

Once levels peak, blood is drawn from the horses, and the plasma is separated and purified into concentrated vials of serum.

The new breakthrough lies in a technique of lyophilisation, or freeze drying, in which the liquid serum is converted into a heat-stable powder.

The antivenom is subjected to a temperature of -40 C inside a deep vacuum chamber. It leaves a fine powder that prevents antibody proteins from degrading or clumping.

Sealed in airtight vials, the powder can sit without refrigeration for years, needing only a splash of sterile water to become an active intravenous antivenom in seconds.

Dr Isabel Batista, Museum Director Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s antivenom infrastructure was the vision of one 19th-century physician.

The Institute’s origins trace back to 1899, when an outbreak of bubonic plague struck Santos, a major port city in the state of São Paulo, threatening Brazil’s coffee-dependent economy.

Officials turned to Dr Vital Brazil, a pioneering physician who set up a makeshift laboratory inside an old stable at Fazenda Butantan, a 400-hectare property outside the capital.

The Institute is not only sharing its life-saving sera, but its world-leading snake research Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To test how the plague spread, he famously let himself be bitten by mosquitoes; when he didn’t fall ill, he (correctly) concluded rodents and fleas, rather than insects, were the vectors.

By 1901, the stables had officially become the Butantan Institute. The research facility was modelled on Paris’s Pasteur Institute – the “global gold-standard reference” of the era, according to Suzana Fernandes, director of the Butantan Center for Cultural Development.

“It was a model adapted here in Brazil for research, production, and the popularisation of science,” she says.

With the plague contained, Dr Brazil turned to a slower, but equally lethal threat: the pit vipers killing thousands of farmers across São Paulo’s booming coffee fields.

The snake conservation enclosure houses critically endangered species Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

While European authorities insisted a single antivenom could treat any bite, Dr Brazil proved serum must be tailored to the snake’s specific genus – a principle that remains foundational to antivenom science today.

To produce these species-specific antivenoms at scale, he devised an unconventional public barter network.

The Institute shipped wooden boxes and snake hooks to rural communities. In return, farmers captured live snakes and loaded them onto trains bound for São Paulo, where conductors guarded the locked crates in dedicated carts.

To seal the bargain, the Institute rewarded those participating with free vials of lifesaving antivenom. Between 1901 and 1977, the railway network delivered over 1.1 million live snakes to Butantan.

More than a century later, new snake lineages are still emerging from Brazil’s vast ecosystems. In 2022, for example, researchers formally described Bothrops jabrensis, a distinct species of pit viper discovered in the high-altitude forests of northeastern Paraíba.

Behind an unmarked door lies Butantan’s Herpetological Collection – one of Latin America’s most important archives of preserved reptiles.

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, curator of the Institute's herpetology collection Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, its curator, leads the way inside, revealing floor-to-ceiling shelves lined with stoppered glass jars. Suspended inside in pale-yellow ethanol are serpents, scorpions, and spiders – their intricate scale patterns and beady eyes frozen mid-glare.

Each jar has a handwritten label – a record of where a species was found, when and by whom. But in 2010, that priceless history was almost wiped out when a devastating fire swept through the Institute, severely damaging its collections.

Between 15,000 and 20,000 specimens were salvaged from the fire Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

Out of what was then the world’s largest snake collection – totaling nearly 100,000 specimens – scientists managed to salvage only 15,000 to 20,000. Most of the glass jars shattered in the intense heat and firefighting efforts.

“We lost more than 100 years of history about snakes in Brazil,” Dr Grazziotin says, adding that the news nearly brought him to tears at the time. “Without the label, a specimen loses its scientific meaning for us. We need to know exactly where it came from”.

A fire at the institute in 2010 severely damaged its herpetological and arachnological collections Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

He walks to the end of one of the solid metal shelves and spins a large mechanical wheel. With a low hum, the wall of jars parts down the middle, opening a new aisle.

As he steps between the banks, Dr Grazziotin points out that despite the devastation of 2010, certain parts of the collection survived the blaze remarkably intact.

“It was purely down to where they were stored in the building,” he says, gesturing toward a meticulously ordered section of jars containing some 8,000 South American rattlesnakes – an entire species’ record preserved against the odds.

Losing a century of history forced Butantan to completely rethink how it preserves its science.

Since the fire, the collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof plastic containers.

In a nearby room, Dr Grazziotin proudly gestures toward a new $2 million (£1.5 million) machine: a sleek Micro-CT scanner, the only one of its kind in South America, he says.

The collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof containers Credit : Camila Svenson

Rather than dissecting rare or historical specimens, it creates non-invasive “digital slices” of snake skulls and internal organs, producing detailed 3D models that can then be analysed online.

The ultimate goal, Dr Grazziotin adds, is to “digitise” the entire 120-year collection into an open-access platform.

The Butantan team is also building a network across Latin America, as well as partnerships with Portuguese-speaking African nations, including Angola and Mozambique.

“We share a language and shared experiences,” Dr Grazziotin says, lifting a nearly two-metre snake from its container. “We are bringing colleagues here to work alongside us, conducting fieldwork over there, and helping them build their own national collections”.

“The idea is to reduce regional disparities,” he adds. “If we can put all the information in our collection online, we can help scientists anywhere in the world”

Brazil’s constitution legally obliges the state to provide treatment regardless of cost, resulting in antivenom having come to be seen as an essential public right, rather than a commodity for profit.

For poor rural workers who cannot afford treatment, receiving free antivenom quickly is what prevents a bite from becoming fatal.

Regional biology helps too. Unlike in Asia or Africa, where dozens of disparate snake families complicate treatment, the dominance of the Bothrops in Brazil makes life easier.

It means that rural clinics only need to stock a few versatile antivenoms rather than dozens of hyper-specialised ones. The Butantan Institute makes roughly 400,000 vials annually, more than enough to meet demand.

Yet even such a well-designed system struggles with the country’s unforgiving geography.

The Butantan Institute is home to Latin America’s largest collection of venomous species Credit : Camila Svenson

Covering nearly half of Brazil, the Amazon rainforest has vast roadless expanses where travel relies on slow wooden boats. For isolated communities, reaching a stocked clinic can take 12 to 24 hours – often beyond the critical window to prevent amputation or death.

Part of the challenge lies in the treatment itself. Traditional liquid antivenom must be administered intravenously under strict medical supervision due to the risk of acute allergic reactions. Crucially, it also requires an unbroken cold chain.

When exposed to tropical heat, the therapeutic proteins quickly denature and clump together. This renders the serum useless or, in the worst cases, dangerous.

Dr Grazziotin holds a tiny snake Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To overcome this, Brazil is increasingly deploying freeze-dried (lyophilised) antivenoms.

Though more expensive and complex to produce, these powder formulations withstand high heat and remain stable for years without cooling, needing only sterile water to reconstitute them for use.

The centuries-old process of creating antivenom is complex and relies on a method barely changed since its invention.

Reptiles at the Institute Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Pioneered in 1895 by French physician Albert Calmette in Saigon (now Ho Chi Minh), Vietnam, the process begins by manually milking live snakes for their venom.

Small, non-lethal doses are then injected into horses over several months, prompting their immune systems to produce high concentrations of specialised antibodies.

Once levels peak, blood is drawn from the horses, and the plasma is separated and purified into concentrated vials of serum.

The new breakthrough lies in a technique of lyophilisation, or freeze drying, in which the liquid serum is converted into a heat-stable powder.

The antivenom is subjected to a temperature of -40 C inside a deep vacuum chamber. It leaves a fine powder that prevents antibody proteins from degrading or clumping.

Sealed in airtight vials, the powder can sit without refrigeration for years, needing only a splash of sterile water to become an active intravenous antivenom in seconds.

Dr Isabel Batista, Museum Director Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Brazil’s antivenom infrastructure was the vision of one 19th-century physician.

The Institute’s origins trace back to 1899, when an outbreak of bubonic plague struck Santos, a major port city in the state of São Paulo, threatening Brazil’s coffee-dependent economy.

Officials turned to Dr Vital Brazil, a pioneering physician who set up a makeshift laboratory inside an old stable at Fazenda Butantan, a 400-hectare property outside the capital.

The Institute is not only sharing its life-saving sera, but its world-leading snake research Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

To test how the plague spread, he famously let himself be bitten by mosquitoes; when he didn’t fall ill, he (correctly) concluded rodents and fleas, rather than insects, were the vectors.

By 1901, the stables had officially become the Butantan Institute. The research facility was modelled on Paris’s Pasteur Institute – the “global gold-standard reference” of the era, according to Suzana Fernandes, director of the Butantan Center for Cultural Development.

“It was a model adapted here in Brazil for research, production, and the popularisation of science,” she says.

With the plague contained, Dr Brazil turned to a slower, but equally lethal threat: the pit vipers killing thousands of farmers across São Paulo’s booming coffee fields.

The snake conservation enclosure houses critically endangered species Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

While European authorities insisted a single antivenom could treat any bite, Dr Brazil proved serum must be tailored to the snake’s specific genus – a principle that remains foundational to antivenom science today.

To produce these species-specific antivenoms at scale, he devised an unconventional public barter network.

The Institute shipped wooden boxes and snake hooks to rural communities. In return, farmers captured live snakes and loaded them onto trains bound for São Paulo, where conductors guarded the locked crates in dedicated carts.

To seal the bargain, the Institute rewarded those participating with free vials of lifesaving antivenom. Between 1901 and 1977, the railway network delivered over 1.1 million live snakes to Butantan.

More than a century later, new snake lineages are still emerging from Brazil’s vast ecosystems. In 2022, for example, researchers formally described Bothrops jabrensis, a distinct species of pit viper discovered in the high-altitude forests of northeastern Paraíba.

Behind an unmarked door lies Butantan’s Herpetological Collection – one of Latin America’s most important archives of preserved reptiles.

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, curator of the Institute's herpetology collection Credit : Camila Svenson/The Telegraph

Dr Felipe Grazziotin, its curator, leads the way inside, revealing floor-to-ceiling shelves lined with stoppered glass jars. Suspended inside in pale-yellow ethanol are serpents, scorpions, and spiders – their intricate scale patterns and beady eyes frozen mid-glare.

Each jar has a handwritten label – a record of where a species was found, when and by whom. But in 2010, that priceless history was almost wiped out when a devastating fire swept through the Institute, severely damaging its collections.

Between 15,000 and 20,000 specimens were salvaged from the fire Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

Out of what was then the world’s largest snake collection – totaling nearly 100,000 specimens – scientists managed to salvage only 15,000 to 20,000. Most of the glass jars shattered in the intense heat and firefighting efforts.

“We lost more than 100 years of history about snakes in Brazil,” Dr Grazziotin says, adding that the news nearly brought him to tears at the time. “Without the label, a specimen loses its scientific meaning for us. We need to know exactly where it came from”.

A fire at the institute in 2010 severely damaged its herpetological and arachnological collections Credit : Marcelo Ribeiro Duarte/Laboratório de Coleções Zoológicas do Instituto Butantan.

He walks to the end of one of the solid metal shelves and spins a large mechanical wheel. With a low hum, the wall of jars parts down the middle, opening a new aisle.

As he steps between the banks, Dr Grazziotin points out that despite the devastation of 2010, certain parts of the collection survived the blaze remarkably intact.

“It was purely down to where they were stored in the building,” he says, gesturing toward a meticulously ordered section of jars containing some 8,000 South American rattlesnakes – an entire species’ record preserved against the odds.

Losing a century of history forced Butantan to completely rethink how it preserves its science.

Since the fire, the collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof plastic containers.

In a nearby room, Dr Grazziotin proudly gestures toward a new $2 million (£1.5 million) machine: a sleek Micro-CT scanner, the only one of its kind in South America, he says.

The collection has been rebuilt inside a state-of-the-art facility with fire-suppression gas systems and shatterproof containers Credit : Camila Svenson

Rather than dissecting rare or historical specimens, it creates non-invasive “digital slices” of snake skulls and internal organs, producing detailed 3D models that can then be analysed online.

The ultimate goal, Dr Grazziotin adds, is to “digitise” the entire 120-year collection into an open-access platform.

The Butantan team is also building a network across Latin America, as well as partnerships with Portuguese-speaking African nations, including Angola and Mozambique.

“We share a language and shared experiences,” Dr Grazziotin says, lifting a nearly two-metre snake from its container. “We are bringing colleagues here to work alongside us, conducting fieldwork over there, and helping them build their own national collections”.

“The idea is to reduce regional disparities,” he adds. “If we can put all the information in our collection online, we can help scientists anywhere in the world”

Sports.title: Man Utd legend’s son scores stunning winner to book team’s place in cup final
Sports.content:
LIAM VAN NISTELROOY is following in his famous father’s footsteps after scoring a stunning winner to send PSV Under-19s into the Otten Innovation Cup final.

The 18-year-old produced a finish straight out of the Ruud van Nistelrooy playbook as PSV beat Chelsea Under-19s 3-1 in the semi-final.



With his proud dad watching from the stands, Liam raced through one-on-one before keeping his cool and calmly dinking the ball over the advancing keeper.

It was a finish that would have looked very familiar to anyone who watched Ruud during his prolific career.



One X user wrote: “He even runs like Ruud. Is gait a genetic trait?”

Former Manchester United Van Nistelrooy striker became a legend at Old Trafford, scoring 150 goals in 219 appearances for the club after arriving from PSV in 2001.

But it was in Eindhoven where Ruud first made his name, smashing 77 goals in just 90 games for PSV before earning his move to England.

He went on to win the Premier League title with United in 2002/03 and claimed the Golden Boot after scoring 25 league goals.



The Dutch striking sensation finished that campaign with 44 goals in all competitions – the second-highest single-season tally in United history, behind only Denis Law‘s 46 in 1963/64.

Now his son appears to have inherited the same deadly instinct in front of goal.

CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

Liam’s cool finish capped a 3-1 victory which booked PSV’s place in the Otten Cup final, where they face Palmeiras Under-19s today.

And there was plenty of United history in the stands as Ruud watched on, having himself enjoyed a fascinating coaching career since hanging up his boots.



Van Nistelrooy served as Erik ten Hag‘s assistant at United at the start of the 2024/25 season before taking temporary charge for four games in October and November 2024.

He then made way for Ruben Amorim after the Portuguese’s appointment as United boss.

A turbulent spell at Leicester City followed as the Foxes went down from the Premier League in 2024/25.

Ruud then went on to work with Holland, serving as Ronald Koeman‘s assistant at the World Cup, where the Dutch were knocked out in the Round of 32 after losing to Morocco on penalties.

Now it is Liam who is beginning to make his own name in football.



Chelsea bounced back from the semi-final defeat by beating Monaco Under-19s 1-0 to claim third place, with Leo Cardoso scoring the winner.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But all eyes will now be on PSV and Liam as they chase Otten Cup glory against Palmeiras.

With a famous surname, a legendary father watching from the stands and a finish straight from the family highlight reel, Liam van Nistelrooy could be destined for big things.

Sports.title: Does Community Shield go to extra time or straight to penalties if Arsenal vs Man City ends as a draw?
Sports.content:
THE Community Shield will take place TODAY as Premier League winners Arsenal take on FA Cup holders Manchester City.

The Gunners were crowned kings of English football for the first time in 22 years last season.



Mikel Arteta‘s men sealed top spot with a game to spare after title rivals City failed to beat Bournemouth in their penultimate match of the campaign.

Pep Guardiola did end this Etihad tenure with two trophies, winning the Carabao Cup and FA Cup.



City beat Arsenal 2-0 in the League Cup showpiece before overcoming Chelsea to win the oldest prize in world football.

Enzo Maresca replaced Guardiola in the hot seat in the blue half of Manchester, and the former Chelsea boss will be looking to kickstart his journey with silverware.

Arsenal are aiming to build winning momentum as Arteta aims to bolster the Gunners’ trophy cabinet.

Today’s match promises fireworks and it could go all the way to decide who takes home the iconic shield.

Does Community Shield go to extra time or straight to penalties if Arsenal vs Man City ends as a draw?

The Community Shield goes straight to penalties if the score is level after 90 minutes.

Since 1993, the Community Shield has gone to spot kicks and is not shared between the teams if it is a draw.



Between 1949 and 1991, the shield was shared 11 times following drawn results.

How to watch the Community Shield

Sports.title: ‘What was that?’ – EFL defender comes on, gives away penalty, makes ‘brutal mistake’ then subbed back off after 12 mins
Sports.content:
LEYTON ORIENT defender James Morris endured a nightmare cameo during his side’s opening day 2-1 defeat to Sheffield Wednesday.

The former Watford full-back started the contest on the bench with Ipswich loanee Somto Boniface preferred at left-back.



Morris, 24, replaced Boniface when the 20-year-old was forced off with an injury on 61 minutes.

After an awful cameo, the defender was himself replaced just 12 minutes later.



Barely five minutes after coming on and with the score level at 1-1, Morris tugged Jamal Lowe down in the box.

Lowe coolly converted from the spot, and things nearly got even worse for Morris just a few minutes later.

As a high ball bounced just inside his own half, hesitant Morris tried to head it back to his goalkeeper Nathan Baxter.

The pass was woefully short, however, allowing Barry Bannan to scurry onto it and round Baxter… only for the Scot to sensationally miss an open goal.

Despite getting away with Morris’ second blunder, boss Richie Wellens had seen enough and decided to replace him with Nicholas Oyekunle.

Orient had gone behind in the first half in similarly farcical circumstances, as keeper Baxter’s clearance struck Callum Slattery and floated in.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

Joseph Olowu equalised on 26 minutes following a cross from a drop ball.

Orient pushed for another leveller late on, but ultimately fell to a 2-1 defeat.

Discussing the match, boss Wellens told the BBC: “First half we saw loads and loads of good signs. We could have scored another couple more, should have scored a couple more

“And then we have a crazy 20 minutes, mistake after mistake. They probably could have scored four or five and it’s all through our mistakes.



“We’re heading it back, we’re passing it back to the goalkeeper, we give a stupid penalty away.

“I’ll take the blame because I probably should have changed it two or three minutes earlier.”

On Morris’ nightmare afternoon, Wellens added “I don’t want to blame anyone, he’s put in, in a difficult period – I’ll take accountability because I should have gone to a back five and give them a little bit of protection on the right hand side.

“When we give a penalty away, and then there’s another mistake, I have to then try and win the game, throw on a more attacking wing-back.

“Morro has done well for us since he signed. He’ll recover from this and he’ll get better.”



Fans couldn’t believe what they had seen from the defender, with one writing on social media: “WHAT was that performance by Morris? He was solid last season and pre-season.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Another brutally added: “James Morris with potentially the worst 10 minute cameo I have ever seen in an Orient shirt…”

Morris will potentially have an opportunity to atone on Tuesday, as Orient host AFC Wimbledon in the EFL Trophy.

Sports.title: Ruben Amorim jokes Man Utd now ‘more boring’ since Michael Carrick replaced him in cheeky exchange
Sports.content:
RUBEN AMORIM aimed a cheeky dig at Manchester United boss Michael Carrick after leading AC Milan to a pre-season win.

The Italian giants notched a 4-2 victory over the Red Devils as preparations were stepped up ahead of the new campaign.



It was the first time Amorim, 41, had gone up against United since being brutally sacked by Old Trafford chiefs in January.

And the clash gave the Portuguese tactician an opportunity to catch up with some familiar faces.



Amorim joked that United’s media briefings have not been as exciting since Carrick was confirmed as his successor.

In a brief exchange with reporters after AC Milan’s win, he asked: “Do you miss me?”



One of the journalists queuing up to speak to Amorim replied: “We miss your press conferences.”

He then burst out laughing before jokingly responding: “They’re more boring now.”

AC Milan’s win over United came a matter of days after they were thumped by Chelsea.

The 3-0 defeat led to Amorim deciding he wants to make wholesale changes to his squad in the final weeks of the transfer window.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

He ruthlessly told SEVEN big-names to find a new club instead of looking to reignite their career at the San Siro.

Christopher Nkunku, Fikayo Tomori, Pervis Estupinan, Santiago Gimenez, Youssouf Fofana, David Odogu and Filippo Terracciano have been put up for sale.

And Amorim pleaded for AC Milan fans to be patient following the mauling against Chelsea.

He said: “We knew we would suffer a little, but we want to put our players through this kind of challenge.

“They know how to defend as a team, play one-on-one and press high. Against teams like Chelsea, we would never press in this way.



“But we are here to prepare ourselves to win the first official match of the season and give the players confidence.

Sports.title: Arsenal vs Man City live stream: How to watch blockbuster Community Shield clash
Sports.content:
LAST season’s title rivals Arsenal and Manchester City go up against each other in a blockbuster Community Shield encounter – and SunSport can reveal where to watch it!

The Gunners ended 22 years of misery by pipping City to the Premier League crown in May.



And as a result, Mikel Arteta‘s men earned themselves a spot in this year’s Community Shield clash.

But ironically, they’ll be taking on Enzo Maresca‘s City side, who will feature after beating Chelsea in last season’s tense FA Cup final.



Whoever comes out on top will gain the psychological edge going into the 2026/27 season.

So you don’t want to miss out on this and all the streaming details are revealed below.



How to watch Arsenal vs Man City in the Community Shield

This year’s Community Shield between Arsenal and Manchester City will be broadcast live on TNT Sports 1.

Fans can also stream the entire action on HBO Max through any compatible device or tablet.

Alternatively, SunSport will have minute-by-minute action of the whole encounter.

When is Arsenal vs Man City in the Community Shield?

Arsenal vs Man City takes place on Sunday, August 16.

The blockbuster match is set to get underway at 3pm BST.

Millennium Stadium, now known as the Principality Stadium in Cardiff, Wales, is the chosen venue for the huge match.

It can host around 73,931 fans for standard rugby union and football events.

Why is the Community Shield being held in Wales?

The Community Shield is usually played at the home of football, Wembley Stadium.

However, in a change to the usual schedule, this year’s game will be played at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff, Wales.

The change comes because Wembley is hosting The Weeknd‘s ‘After Hours til Dawn’ tour on the same day.

This year will be the third time since the stadium reopened in 2007 that the Community Shield will take place away from London.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi misses third straight penalty on horror night as Inter Miami routed and GOAT has ref row and freak miss
Sports.content:
LIONEL MESSI endured a night to forget as Inter Miami fell to a 4-1 thrashing at the hands of Nashville in the MLS.

The GOAT is back playing club football in the US following the World Cup and the heartbreaking loss of his father.



But he is still clearly not himself on the pitch as he suffered a bizarre series of misfortunes on a nightmare night in Nashville.

Not least among the calamities was yet another penalty miss – the third time in a row the Argentina legend has failed to convert from the spot.



The 39-year-old had the chance to level the score at 1-1 in the 23rd minute, but his tame effort was blocked by the goalkeeper down to his right side.

Former Manchester United and Spurs star Sergio Reguilon turned in the rebound, before the goal was chalked off for encroachment.



It was Messi’s third missed spot kick in a row, having failed to score attempts in matches against Egypt and Austria at the World Cup.

And his struggles didn’t end there in the clash, which constituted a third consecutive loss for the David Beckham-backed outfit.

Messi was sure he was fouled in the build-up to former Nottingham Forest star Sam Surridge‘s goal.

But his fierce complaints to the referee only earned him a yellow card for dissent.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

With that incident still fresh in his mind, and after Hany Mukhtar added Nashville’s fourth goal of the night, Messi might have thought he had found his breakthrough when he latched onto a ball in the box in added time.

His initial effort cannoned off the right post, only to bounce right back into his path, where he tried to steer it goalwards again only for it to this time hit the left post.

And as a cherry on top of a disastrous evening for the Barcelona icon, he finally scored just minutes later only for that finish to be cancelled out for offside.

Sports.title: Controversial ex-Newcastle star Nile Ranger to make boxing debut on same fight card as former Brentford captain
Sports.content:
FORMER Newcastle striker Nile Ranger is swapping the football pitch for the boxing ring.

The ex-Premier League forward has been confirmed as a fighter for the third edition of charity boxing event A Night to Remember.



Ranger, 35, will lace up the gloves at London’s JW Marriott Grosvenor House on October 22 as part of a card featuring a host of former footballers.

And he will be joined on the bill by former Brentford captain Harlee Dean, who is also preparing to trade tackles for punches.



Organisers Pro Project Promotions announced Ranger’s involvement on Instagram, writing: “Proud to announce that @nilepowerranger [Instagram handle] is a confirmed fighter for A Night To Remember III.”

They added: “From the football pitch to the ring, Nile is stepping into a new challenge and will be putting it all on the line in London this October.”

Dean, 35, was unveiled separately, with the former Bees skipper having also represented Birmingham City, Reading and Sheffield Wednesday during his career.

The defender made almost 249 appearances for Brentford and captained the club before leaving for Birmingham in 2017, building a reputation as a commanding presence at the back.

But Ranger arrives with a far more controversial history after a career which promised plenty but was repeatedly overshadowed by problems away from football.

The striker broke into Newcastle’s first team as a highly-rated youngster and helped the Magpies win promotion back to the Premier League in 2010.



But disciplinary problems and a series of legal issues subsequently followed.

Ranger has previously served prison sentences and received criminal convictions during a turbulent career.

Ranger currently plays as a striker for AFC Whyteleafe, a non-league football club competing in the Isthmian League Premier Division.



He officially signed with the club yesterday, making his debut almost immediately in a 2–2 draw against Wingate & Finchley.

The move marks his fourth club transfer in just two years, following brief recent stints with other semi-pro outfits like Kettering Town, Wellingborough Town, and Chatham Town.

A Night to Remember is the brainchild of former Arsenal goalkeeper Graham Stack and sees ex-professional footballers step inside the ring for charity.

Its inaugural event in London in October 2025 raised more than £125,000, with former Chelsea midfielder Jody Morris beating ex-Tottenham star David Bentley by unanimous decision.

The series returned for a second show in Liverpool earlier this year and the third instalment heads back to Grosvenor House in October.



With organisers aiming to drive their fundraising towards £500,000 for causes including the Willow Foundation and Sport in Mind.

Sports.title: Marcus Rashford’s future at Man Utd remains uncertain with Harry Maguire making case why transfer exit must be rejected
Sports.content:
HARRY MAGUIRE revealed that his Manchester United teammates “hope” Marcus Rashford stays at Old Trafford.

The forward ended a 611-day absence for his boyhood club, coming on after 61 minutes in United’s 4-2 loss to Ruben Amorim’s Milan in Wroclaw.



But the England star’s future remains uncertain, despite sources suggesting that he will likely recommit to United.

Carrick had every chance to confirm Rashford’s future during Thursday’s sitdown in Maynooth, yet stopped short of guaranteeing he would remain beyond the end of the month.



When asked about Rashford’s qualities on Saturday, Maguire took the initiative to address his teammate’s future.

Maguire, 33, said: “He’s a huge threat, he’s a huge threat to have in your team. So if he’s going to stay with us, obviously the transfer window is still open, but we hope as players that he stays and he’s a big asset to have.

“I’ve played with Marcus for numerous years and I know that playing against him and with him in training is going to help us.

“He can improve us. When you see when he comes on, he threatens the back line really well. He could have even scored for us today.”

United officials quickly made it known that the number nine shirt Rashford wore in Poland was not permanent, sparing potential buyers any future frustration.

It marked his first appearance for United since the Europa League tie against Viktoria Plzen on December 12 2024. Banished by Amorim soon after, successive loan spells at Aston Villa and Barcelona seemed to signal the end of his time at the club.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Rashford’s first run run ended in a foul, but he quickly redeemed himself by dazzling a defender near the corner flag with a brilliant piece of footwork.

As the club’s highest earner, his return is a factor in why United’s transfer business has stalled since Youri Tielemans’ £35m arrival from Villa.

United desperately need a left back and have had two first stage enquiries for Lewis Hall knocked back by Newcastle.

Maguire’s header put United ahead inside two minutes before Patrick Dorgu regained the lead.



Despite tensions between Amorim and Rashford, many United players held their former manager in high regard.

Following the trophy presentation, Bruno Fernandes, Luke Shaw, Noussair Mazraoui, Lisandro Martínez, and Joshua Zirkzee were among the first to embrace him.

Maguire said: “It’s great to see him. Great to see him and all his staff. I’m happy that they’re in another job and another chance to impress and to show everyone what a great manager he is.

“So I have nothing bad to say about Ruben. I got on with Ruben really, really well and all his staff. I’m sure he’s going to be a success, it just didn’t work out at Manchester United.

“But when you’re a manager and you put yourself in that firing seat, there’s going to be disappointments and he’ll be disappointed it didn’t.



“But he’s got a massive club now in AC Milan and myself, I wish him and all his staff the very best. I’ll be following them and I hope they have an amazing season.”

Kobbie Mainoo and World Cup finalist Lisandro Martinez made their first pre-season appearances, while skipper Bruno Fernandes and Youri Tielemans both went the full 90 minutes.

Amorim’s side, using the 3-4-2-1 system that proved an ill fit at United, blew United away in the second half.

Samuel Chukwueze, who spent last season on loan at Fulham, constantly found joy at right wing-back, setting up Alphadjo Cisse and Goncalo Ramos with two identical crosses from Luke Shaw‘s side.

Maguire insisted United will be ready for their Prem opener against Hull City on Saturday, despite what he called their “worst performance in pre-season“.



He said: “It’s a week before the season and these games can become a little bit passive. It felt like a pre-season friendly if I’m being honest.

“It was at a slow tempo and credit to Milan, they played at a higher tempo than us and they were a little bit more aggressive than us and they probably deserved the win in the end.

“We’ll be ready to go, that’s the Premier League. 12:30 on a Saturday away at Hull, it’s going to be an intense game and one that we’re ready to go.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I don’t want to find excuses, but of course it’s the last game before, and there’s probably boys out there wanting to make sure that they get through the game and get the minutes into the legs without pushing too intensely to be ready next week.

“But it wasn’t a good performance from us, we know that. We’ve got to do better, we’ve got to improve, but we’ve got a full week to analyse and we will do.”

Sports.title: Victor Osimhen to Arsenal decision made by Galatasaray after 'private internal transfer talks'
Sports.content:
Victor Osimhen to Arsenal decision made by Galatasaray after 'private internal transfer talks'

Arsenal have been linked with a move for Victor Osimhen, but the Gunners face a tough battle to secure the £58m-rated Galatasaray striker

View 2 Images Victor Osimhen is on the list of Arsenal targets this summer. (Image: Ahmad Mora/Getty Images)

The president of Turkish giants Galatasaray has reportedly made clear Arsenal target Victor Osimhen isn't for sale. Mikel Arteta is said to be determined to bring the 27-year-old talisman to north London as part of the plans to successfully defend their Premier League crown.

‌



However, claims suggest Dursun Ozbek has told his insiders that the Nigerian is not for sale under any circumstances. Osimhen helped catapult the Istanbul side to more league success last season and scored a brace, including a stoppage-time equaliser, as they salvaged a point on the opening day against newly-promoted opposition.

‌



While Arsenal secured marquee signing Bruno Guimaraes and recruited Christos Tzolis as a replacement for Leandro Trossard, they fell short in their pursuit of both Vinicius Junior and Morgan Rogers.

‌



It has been suggested that Arsenal have shifted their focus towards Osimhen as hopes of landing Atletico Madrid's Julian Alvarez continue to fade. Yet a deal for the 27-year-old may prove equally complicated, with the Galatasaray president reportedly reiterating behind closed doors that Osimhen remains firmly off the market.

343 Digital report that Ozbek told insiders: "I will not say 'yes' to any transaction that will harm Galatasaray or not benefit Galatasaray. What I said about Baris Alper Yilmaz, I am now saying even more strongly about Osimhen. No matter how much the price is, I am not selling Osimhen."

FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



It comes as little shock that the Istanbul club are keen to retain the striker following his impressive haul of 22 goals across all competitions last season. Osimhen bagged 15 league goals during Galatasaray's title-winning campaign, and the 27-year-old made an immediate impact in their opening league fixture at the weekend.

The forward struck twice, including a last-gasp equaliser, in the draw with Corum FK.

He remained tight-lipped about his future following the opening-night draw against last season's play-off winners.

‌



He said: "There are always rumours in transfer seasons. I will take care of my business. I am focused on my job, then we will see and think further."

View 2 Images Arsenal face a task in convincing Galatasaray into the sale of Victor Osimhen. (Image: Ferda Demir, Getty Images)

Arsenal could find themselves having to match the fee Galatasaray paid Napoli to secure Osimhen's signature. The Turkish giants shelled out around €70million (£58m) for his services.

‌



French reports have suggested the Gunners may need to part with a minimum of £58m, with Foot Mercato claiming earlier this week that Arsenal remain confident of getting a deal over the line before the window shuts.

Osimhen has never hidden his desire to test himself in the Premier League, with the likes of Chelsea circling for his signature back in 2023. The prolific striker said at the time: "I think playing in one of the top five leagues in the world is an amazing feeling for me.

"A lot of people worldwide consider the Premier League as the best and the strongest league but now I'm in one of the best leagues in the world which is the Italian Serie A.

"I'm working so hard to make sure that I achieve my dream of playing in the Premier League some day but like I said, it's a process and I just want to keep on this momentum and continue to do well."

Sports.title: Transfer news LIVE: Liverpool's Barcola boost, £60m for Arsenal to sign star, double Spurs deal
Sports.content:
All of the latest transfer news from the Premier League and further afield, including updates on Arsenal, Liverpool, Manchester United, Tottenham Hotspur and more

Hello and welcome to Mirror Football's transfer live blog for Sunday, August 16.

Liverpool have been handed a major boost in their pursuit of Bradley Barcola as a result of Paris Saint-Germain signing Mika Godts from Ajax. There was speculation that the Ligue 1 champions would be willing to trim their £145million valuation of the 23-year-old, but only if they secured a solid replacement on the left.

Having done so, it's now a waiting game to see whether the rumour mill has churned truth with regards to a potential cut-price deal for Barcola. The Frenchman has been a priority target for Liverpool for the majority of the summer, as Andoni Iraola looks for further firepower up the top end of the pitch to challenge in 2026/27.

Arsenal, meanwhile, may have to fork out at least £60m if they hope to sign Galatasaray's Victor Osimhen before next month's transfer deadline, according to sources speaking with Football Insider.

The Gunners are also looking for attacking threat this summer, having missed out on Real Madrid's Vinicius Junior following a long and drawn out transfer saga. They could now turn their attention to 27-year-old Osimhen, who has been linked with a move to the Premier League for the past couple of years, only for a deal to fail to come to fruition.

On the other side of North London, Tottenham Hotspur are eyeing moves for Liverpool's Cody Gakpo and Manchester City's Savinho, as a summer of massive spending continues. Reports from the Netherlands suggest that Gakpo has reached an agreement in principle with regards to personal terms, with a £70m price tag being touted for his transfer.

Savinho, meanwhile, has reportedly shared an interest in working under Roberto De Zerbi this season, with Spurs looking to wrap up an £85m move for the Brazilian.

At the Etihad Stadium, the Cityzens are on the brink of securing Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille in an £85m swoop of their own, as Rodri closes in on a move to Barcelona. Having already welcomed Elliot Anderson in a £116m transfer from Nottingham Forest, City have now turned their attention to finding a suitable playing partner for the 23-year-old.

Bouaddi, 18, could be just that, following a formidable World Cup campaign with Morocco.

Sports.title: Ex-Arsenal star announces retirement hours before Community Shield after ‘suffering’ for years
Sports.content:
Ex-Arsenal star announces retirement hours before Community Shield after ‘suffering’ for years

A former Arsenal star of the best part of a decade has announced his retirement from the beautiful game with a highly-emotional statement

View 2 Images Carl Jenkinson shared his announcement of retirement online (Image: David Price, Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

Carl Jenkinson has shared an emotional statement on social media to confirm his retirement from football. The 33-year-old kicked off his career at the Charlton youth academy, before breaking into the first team in 2010.

‌



A transfer to Arsenal then ensued a year later, where he remained for eight years before joining Nottingham Forest in 2019. After a three-year spell at the City Ground, Jenkinson then transferred to Newcastle Jets.

‌



He finished his playing days with Bromley between 2024 and 2026, before leaving the club as a free agent upon the expiration of his contract in May. And now, he has called time on an admirable career under the bright lights.

‌



Seven players will miss Arsenal vs Man City Community Shield final READ MORE :

Writing on X, Jenkinson said: "Thank you to everyone who played a part in my journey, from my Charlton days as a kid through to my last time playing football at Bromley. From the age of 8 football has been my life, it's given me a lot, and I have also given it a lot back.

"In fact I've given it everything. It's for that reason that I can write this looking back over my career with no regrets. Do I wish certain things went better? Without a doubt. A lot of things.

"I once scored an own goal from 30 yards out. I certainly wouldn't mind deleting that from history. But were these bad or difficult moments ever because of a lack of effort? No. Like I said, I gave football everything. Everyday. And I guess I'm writing this because I can see that's getting lost a bit these days."

‌



"I don't know if it's social media painting a certain picture of what a footballer looks like, but I want to be clear, behind the scenes these top players train like their life depends on it. Alexis Sánchez, wow. Every training session he trained like it was his last.

"The ones that don't, they fall by the way side eventually. Even when they're really, really good. I've seen it happen to too many young pros and scholars, trying to make a name in the game. Apply yourself everyday, listen to your coaches and learn from the players who have already been where you want to get to.

"Because if you don't make it, and it's because you got carried away with yourself, it'll be a heavy burden to carry later in life. I suffered a lot with confidence throughout my career, which I found strange because my Dad always backs himself to the hilt.

"I saw loads of people, to try and unlock something within me and find that inner belief. 'Take the chains off,' Arsène Wenger would say to me. 'I'm trying boss,' I would say to myself. But I'm certain it was that same insecurity that gave me the drive I have, that would make me run harder and train harder than everyone else.

‌



"Ultimately that's what gave me a career at the top level, because physically I was a machine and I took a lot of pride in that. Was the way I am a blessing or a curse for me? A bit of both I think.

View 2 Images Carl Jenkinson has retired (Image: PA)

"But you can only play the cards you're dealt and try and make the best of them. I'm writing all this because I hope some young players might read it. You guys have so much confidence these days!

‌



"I wish I could nick some of it and take it back in time, but confidence without application and having that fire in your belly to improve everyday won't get you far. I see less young players doing extras, working on their craft, doing extra running after training.

"Trust me, you won't have a career if you neglect this aspect. Try and find the sweetspot.

‌



"That's why I love guys like Bukayo Saka. He's got that swagger, but you only need to listen to him in a post match interview to see he's never lost his humility. Find the sweetspot. Hopefully the above has some value to someone out there.

"I didn't want to write the generic retirement 'thanks for everything,' post as it seemed like a missed opportunity. Although of course I am very grateful to my friends, family, coaches, managers and of course the fans who have been with me on my journey.

"I'm looking forward to seeing what life has in store for me next. Cheers, Jenko."

Sports.title: Precise faces More Thunder in Prix Jacques le Marois
Sports.content:
Precise, More Thunder and Zeus Olympios line up for the 2026 Prix Jacques Le Marois, live on Sky Sports Racing.

2.50 Deauville - Precise takes on More Thunder and Zeus Olympios in Prix Jacques le Marois

Star filly Precise takes on More Thunder and Zeus Olympios in a very competitive renewal of the The Aga Khan Studs Prix Jacques le Marois.

Four-time Group 1 winner Precise has built herself a very nice profile, having backed up a pair of Group 1 wins at two with victories in the Irish 1000 Guineas and Coronation Stakes. She has since been beaten twice since stepping into open company, being downed by the Juddmonte-owned Blue Bolt on both occasions. The fillies' allowance could prove crucial here and with Ryan Moore on board, she is in the right hands.

More Thunder will look to reverse the form with Zeus Olympios, with the latter much the best when last seen in Ascot's Summer Mile. Karl Burke's charge got the run of the race that day, scooting clean under Sam James. William Haggas' representative was second in Group 1 company twice prior and, like Zeus Olympios, will look to take top honours for the first time today.

Thesecretadversary is a recent Group 1 scorer in the Prix Jean Prat, which followed a win at the Royal meeting in the Jersey Stakes. He was originally targeted towards the City Of York Stakes but has since been rerouted after Bow Echo and Gstaad were retired and ruled out respectively.

Rayif looks the best of the French contenders but will have to bounce back after disappointing when sent off a 6/4 favourite in the Prix Jean Prat. The step back up to a mile could prove crucial for Mickael Barzalona's mount, who tasted success over the mile in the French 2000 Guineas earlier this season.

1.33 Deauville - Exciting Avec Toi faces Silver Dominion in Group 3 company

The much talked about Avec Toi faces just four runners in this Group 3 The Aga Khan Studs Prix Francois Boutin.

Christopher Head has said the target this season for this son of No Nay Never is the Prix Jean-Luc Lagardere on Arc weekend and he looks to be a special talent from his outings thus far. He arrives here with two wins from as many starts, with a debut win at Saint-Cloud followed up by a sparkling showing over this course and distance the last day.

In opposition, Silver Dominion brings stakes form to the table. Oliver Cole's runner finished second in the Pat Eddery Stakes last time after a fourth-place finish in the Superlative Stakes on July Cup day and could give the favourite a real run for his money.

Godolphin's Jassas looked promising when winning on debut at Doncaster - a result which has seen the form boosted this week with runner-up Narrjoo winning at Ffos Las on Wednesday. Zakkan cannot be discounted for the formidable Graffard and Barzalona combination despite being winless in three, whilst Cut A Dash completes the quintet and looks to have plenty to find on the rest of the field.

2.35 Southwell - 750,000gns Godolphin yearling Palladas returns

Expensive yearling Palladas returns to the track for the LNAA Critical Care Novice Stakes after being absent since beating Al Azd at Kempton in January.

The form from this maiden victory has produced seven individual winners - most notably Al Azd, who is now rated 109. Roger Varian's Shadwell gelding was sixth in the London Gold Cup and second in the King George V Stakes before hosing up at Ascot in a class 2 handicap. That form line would suggest a lofty ceiling for Charlie Appleby's runner today, who will be partnered by the title-chasing Billy Loughnane.

Theory Of Tides' half-brother Mercantile debuts for Daniel and Clare Kubler and is of interest first time out, but this should really be a one-horse race.

Best of the rest

Back at Deauville, Listed winner Romantic Symphony goes in search of Group 3 honours in the The Aga Khan Studs Prix Lady O'Reilly. She will be rivalled by Calandagan's half-sister Calasita, who holds an entry in the Champions Fillies And Mares Stakes and was only half a length behind Romantic Symphony last time. Dispatches drops down into Group 3 company under Colin Keane, whilst Hatanka Fal has been there or thereabouts at Listed level but must improve to go close today.

At Southwell, Astrological looks to carry a 6lb penalty to success in the Newark Advertiser Handicap (1.30pm) before Valvano and Legal Reform clash in the Coopers Marquees Handicap at 3.40pm.

Sports.title: Scheffler retains lead in Memphis as Burns stars and McIlroy toils again
Sports.content:
Scottie Scheffler will take a two-shot lead into the final round of the FedEx St Jude Championship in Memphis as he looks to complete his first win since January.

The three-stroke advantage the world No 1 had carved out at halfway after a second-round, course-record 61 was trimmed by one as he bogeyed his penultimate hole at TPC Southwind on Saturday before signing for a two-under 68 and closing on 13 under.

Sam Burns carded a sizzling, bogey-free eight-under 62 while Sungjae Im shot a three-under 67 with those players the leader's closest challengers on 11 under.

But Scheffler is now just one good day away from his maiden trophy since The American Express in California at the start of the year, not that he hasn't threatened in that time.

How do the FedExCup Playoffs work? Only the top 70 in the season-long FedExCup standings have reached the FedEx St. Jude Championship. The top 50 then progress to the BMW Championship (August 20-23) and then only the top 30 make it to the Tour Championship (August 27-30). Winners of the first two play-off events earn 750 points apiece before the points reset to zero ahead of the Tour Championship. In the closing event, all players begin at even par, with the starting-strokes model based on FedExCup placings at that point axed in 2025. The winner of the Tour Championship becomes FedExCup champion for 2026, earning $10m (£7.4m) and a five-year PGA Tour exemption.

The 30-year-old has recorded five runners-up finishes, including at the 3M Open in his previous event, and nine top-fives in total in the intervening months.

In his third round in Tennessee, Scheffler bogeyed his fourth hole before birdies at two, 11, 12 and 16 preceded that dropped shot at 17, which came after he picked out a left-hand bunker with his second shot at the par four.

Defending FedExCup Playoffs champion Tommy Fleetwood remains in the hunt after a two-under Saturday - the highlight of which was a monster birdie putt at 13 - leaving him five strokes adrift of Scheffler on eight under and in a share of fourth with Jake Knapp.

Image: Rory McIlroy has not shot a round under par at TPC Southwind this week

Rory McIlroy, though, is languishing in tied-67th place on six over - 19 shots off Scheffler - after shooting a two-over 72 on Saturday, with the world No 2 yet to post an under-par round this week.

McIlroy, a three-time FedExCup Playoffs champion, was even par on the day heading to the 18th in his third round, only to then finish with a double bogey after finding the water off the tee.

The 37-year-old picked up back-to-back birdies at nine and 10, while his bogeys came at two and 13 before his gory final hole.

Sports.title: Djokovic struggles with heat in Cincinnati as Wimbledon hero Fery returns
Sports.content:
Novak Djokovic suffered defeat and struggled physically in his first match since Wimbledon as he was upset by Thiago Agustin Tirante in a sapping three-set contest at the Cincinnati Open.

Djokovic, inactive on the ATP Tour since losing to Jannik Sinner at the grass-court Grand Slam on July 10, won the first set 6-2 but then lost the next two 6-4 as he battled the heat and humidity in Ohio, even appearing to vomit at one stage.

The 24-time major champion won an 18-minute third game of the second set, fending off four break points over nine deuces, before taking a medical timeout, while he dropped to his hands and knees at certain points in a match that lasted two hours and 45 minutes.

Tirante revels in 'best win of career'

Tirante, who can look forward to a third-round meeting with Spain's Martin Landaluce, made the decisive break at 4-4 in the decider after converting his fourth break point of the game and then closed out the win on serve.

Image: Tirante says his win over Djokovic was the best of his career

He said afterwards: "This is the best win of my career. I really did a good job inside the court. I managed very well the nerves of playing against a legend like Novak. Now I feel relieved.

"It is all so much pressure when you cannot break [serve]. I had so many points to break and I couldn't, so that was the key. Keep believing in myself with my team and think about it after the match."

Djokovic was the third seed in Cincinnati despite sitting fifth in the world rankings, with world No 1 Sinner withdrawing due to a knee injury and world No 3 Carlos Alcaraz also absent as he continues to deal with a lingering wrist issue.

Norrie beaten by top-seed Zverev | Fery wins

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the Cincinnati Open match between Cameron Norrie vs Dino Prizmic

Elsewhere, in a rain-delayed match that finished at 2:15am local time on Sunday, top seed Alexander Zverev rallied to avoid a third straight defeat, beating Cameron Norrie 3-6 6-3 6-3.

Zverev, the French Open champion, had returned to action in Montreal after losing to Jannik Sinner in the Wimbledon final, but suffered a first-round defeat by Tallon Griekspoor.

Meanwhile, Wimbledon semi-finalist Arthur Fery advanced with a hard-fought 6-4, 2-6, 7-6 victory over James Duckworth.

Britain's Boulter crashes out

British No 2 Katie Boulter saw her campaign end in the second round with a 6-3 6-3 defeat to Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova.

Noskova, who served 10 aces compared to Boulter's none, converted four of the nine break points she fashioned and was only broken once in return.
