World.title: Haddara crime family boss shot in Altona North
World.content:
Police are investigating after a man believed to be the alleged one-time gangland boss Fadi Haddara was shot in Altona North this evening. Police and Haddara’s lawyer have been contacted for comment. Fadi Haddara Jason South The Age has heard from multiple sources that Haddara was shot at while parked in a car in his driveway on Marigold Avenue near Millers Road and is now receiving treatment at the Royal Melbourne Hospital. He is believed to be in a stable, non-life-threatening condition.



Related Article Exclusive

Crime When the head of a crime family found trackers on his car, he knew the game was up Haddara, alleged patriarch of the Haddara crime family, once held a commanding position over the illicit tobacco trade in Melbourne but had been squeezed out by new gangland boss Kazem “Kaz” Hamad in early 2024. The Age has previously reported that the Haddaras surrendered their stake in the illicit tobacco smuggling and distribution market following a relentless firebombing and shooting campaign waged by Hamad in 2023-2024, including Fadi finding multiple GPS trackers on his car. The attack on Fadi has been met with surprise in the underworld given the clan was largely sidelined following Hamad’s establishment of cartel-like control over the tobacco market. Attempts by some criminal players to take advantage of Hamad’s arrest in Iraq in January have met with acts of serious retribution by Hamad’s gang, known as The Commission or the 313.



From left: Waleed Haddara, Fadi Haddara, Sam Abdulrahim and his trainer Pierre Karam. Instagram Four businesses and a home owned or linked to the crime gang led by Haddara were attacked in March of this year alone, including the torching of the Capriccio Gelateria in Williamstown and a drive-by shooting targeting a crowd of men standing outside an Altona North kebab shop in the heart of the gang’s territory. Emergency services were at the house on Sunday night where Haddara was shot. Alleged gangland boss Fadi Haddara. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: From pasta pastor to plastic projectile
World.content:
Barrie Restall of Teven thinks “if Les Shearman of Darlington, a Pastafarian (C8), is exploring new religions he might like to try Frisbitarianism, the belief that when you die you go up onto the roof and get stuck there”.

Actually, this time around, Les took a more automated approach: “I got AI to fill in my census. For religion, it put AIthiest.”

“A young zealot tried to convince me of his religious beliefs,” says Wendy Crew of Lane Cove North. “I told him I had none, and in fact was against all religion. His prompt and unyielding response was ‘Well, that’s your religion!’”

It’s a heartache for Adrian Bell of Davistown: “Dare I suggest that the recent total eclipse might have been a celestial tribute to the sad loss of Bonnie Tyler?”

“We had a stopover in Singapore on the way to England in 1974,” recalls Rob Jackson of Cheltenham. “Our family, consisting of me, my wife, two girls and one boy, were detained by a customs official and my hair (C8), reaching beneath my collar as it was, was declared to be inadmissible. My wife set about cutting it with some small scissors she had in her handbag. Soon some students from our plane asked if she could perform the same operation for them, which she duly did. Others wore low T-shirts and were allowed through, despite having longer hair. Our five-year-old daughter, who had very long, fair hair, asked apprehensively if she had to have hers cut, too, but was assured that she didn’t.”

World.title: Kaikōura trust seeks review after DOC decides not to vaccinate penguins amidst bird flu
World.content:
The Kaikōura Wildlife Centre Trust is seeking ministerial review of the Department of Conservation's decision not to vaccinate little penguins against bird flu.

Australian media reported that a little penguin on Phillip Island had died from the virus.

The Department of Conservation's H5 bird flu programme lead Suliana Teasdale said its vaccination programme focused on up to 30 threatened bird species that were considered at high risk from H5 bird flu and faced a risk of extinction if the virus had a significant impact.

"These species generally have small populations. Kororā do not meet these criteria. If the disease risk for kororā changes, DOC will adapt its management strategies, as planned for all species at risk from H5 bird flu," she said.

A malnourished kororā chick receiving in situ supplemental feeding by Trust Manager Sabrina Luecht. Kaikoura Wildlife Centre Trust/Supplied

The Kaikōura Wildlife Centre Trust's Manager Sabrina Luecht said that approach was short sighted.

She said little penguins were at risk of mass localised extinctions.

"If we do not act in terms of vaccinations we will lose these birds within a season or two. It will be total extinction because of the starvation impacts that already exist," she said.

Soft released kororā fledglings post artificial rearing and rehabilitation Kaikoura Wildlife Centre Trust/Supplied

Luecht added that Kaikōura kororā presented an exceptional case.

"For a remnant population of 50 kororā on the brink of regional extinction, faced with severe existing pressures such as starvation, a HPAI (highly pathogenic avian influenza) outbreak will have unprecedented consequences from which the population simply cannot recover," she said.

Luecht said DOC had not considered the Kaikōura kororā's extreme vulnerability, existing extinction threat and small population size.

A 7 week old malnourished kororā chick being weighed during a welfare check. Kaikoura Wildlife Centre Trust/Supplied

"In the wake of HPAI spreading, Australia is planning to vaccinate thousands of little penguins in the state of Victoria. This makes for an excellent comparative case, for why New Zealand should be vaccinating feasible kororā populations at sites such as Kaikōura in New Zealand," she said.

"DOC cannot simply ignore this critically time sensitive issue any further, nor argue against the need and viability of implementing a kororā vaccination programme."

Reserves have been implemented and managed by the Trust as safe zones off limits to the public. Kaikoura Wildlife Centre Trust/Supplied

The Department of Conservation's Suliana Teasdale said the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) had approved tranche 2 of its vaccination plan, which would allow it to extend vaccination to up to 25 additional priority species where it would provide the greatest protection.

"Planning for this work is underway. We are currently working through which species will be vaccinated in tranche 2. Before making final decisions, we are engaging with mana whenua and stakeholders and continuing to assess the risk to those species as the H5 bird flu situation evolves in New Zealand," she said.

Minister for Conservation Tama Potaka said MPI-approved vaccination for wild birds was currently limited to threatened bird species, considered to be at high risk from the bird flu.

"DOC's vaccination programme is currently focused on up to 30 threatened bird species. Kororā do not meet the criteria for the vaccination under the current approval which I recognise may be disappointing for the Trust and some members of the community."

Potaka said he acknowledged the Trust's work support the resilience of Kaikōura kororā with its predator control, encouraging them to continue their efforts.

World.title: Hamilton knife attack puts four people in hospital
World.content:
Police in Waikato are describing last night's stabbing of four people at a house in Maeroa as a large-scale incident, spread over several properties.

One person is in hospital with critical injuries, while two others suffered non-life-threatening but serious injuries. A fourth person has minor injuries.

Inspector Karl Thornton says police were alerted to the incident on Churchill Avenue just before 9pm on Saturday and arrested a 23-year-old man.

He is due to appear in the Hamilton District Court tomorrow facing assault charges.

Police said as the attack unfolded, one victim fled on foot to seek help at a nearby property and was followed there by the offender.

RNZ / Rachel Moore

It is alleged that an occupant there fired a gun, but caused no injury.

Rhiannon Connor who lives on Churchill Avenue, said she had heard screaming on Saturday night as the incident unfolded.

"I heard like bang, bang, bang, bang, bang, and I was like, holy f***, what's that?"

Connor was worried the person would show up at her house next.

Police are not seeking anyone else in relation to the incident.

Thornton said residents can expect to see extra police in the area over the next few days.

Hamilton West MP Tama Potaka said he was deeply concerned by the serious incident in Maeroa.

"My thoughts are with those who have been injured, their whānau and everyone in the community affected by what happened. I want to acknowledge police and emergency services for their response."

World.title: Tourists causing headaches on Instagrammable rural road in Taranaki
World.content:
Instagrammable rural scene causing headache for locals Country Life Download MP3 5m

Dairy farmer Amanda Jordan lives in view of arguably one of the world's most beautiful sights, Mount Taranaki. It's a magnet for people wanting to stop for the perfect photo - and they do.

Jordan told RNZ's Country Life podcast that people in the area fear someone could die while taking photos on Kent Road for social media.

"People that don't know our roads... they want that perfect photo of the mountain or a perfect photo of the sheep and you come around a corner and you come across people standing on the road," she said.

"For a few years, there's been a lot of near misses on that hill because it's a blind hill.

"Things could go wrong pretty quickly."

Locals saw tourists from across the country and overseas stopping for photos. Jordan said there had even been reports of people lying in the road.

The area had been used for wedding photos over the years too, but that was well managed, Jordan said.

"They'll have spotters on both sides of the hill to stop traffic so the bride can beautify her dress and come out and have the beautiful photo," she said.

"You don't mind that so much because you know the risk is over the hill because you've got someone stopping it."

It was different when there were 10 cars parked on the sides of the roads, with up to 15 people taking photos, Jordan said.

"Police do get called every now and then, but within an hour, if it's a nice fine day, you've got a different group of people."

Kent Road in Taranaki RNZ/Sally Round

The rise of electric cars had made things even worse, due to how quiet the vehicles are. Jordan said those stopping for photos "won't even hear you coming on the other side of the hill".

"Our car's not very loud so I have to be particularly careful because they can't hear us," she said.

Yellow dotted lines have been put in place along the sides of the roads. Signs telling people not to stop had been installed as well.

Those measures had not worked and more needed to be done, Jordan said. Caution was needed to ensure whatever they did did not just shift the problem elsewhere, she added.

"I think we probably need to publicise that there's actually a beautiful spot down at Lake Mangamahoe.

"There is a lookout that you can walk up ... it's not an arduous walk, just up on a hill.

"You get the same beautiful photo of the mountain, but you've also got the beautiful Lake Mangamahoe in that photo as well," she said.

In July, police warned members of the public not to put themselves at risk on the road for a photo.

Senior Sergeant Matt Prendergast said motorists had reported almost hitting people who had stopped for photos.

"Concerningly, people are ignoring the signs and have been seeing lying on the road and stopping traffic to take photos of the mountain," he said.

"We've had more than one report of people nearly being hit, and multiple near misses being reported.

"People are not only endangering themselves, but all road users.

"We can't always be there to enforce the law, so we are appealing to people to use their common sense and obey the signs. It is not worth risking your life to update your social media account," he said.

A petition calling for action over the problem has been presented to the New Plymouth District Council.

World.title: Twelve killed and at least 10 injured in Polish bus crash in Hungary
World.content:
A dozen people were killed and at least 10 have been injured injured after a Polish bus overturned at night on a motorway in eastern Hungary, Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar says.

The bus ran into a ditch and tipped over early on Sunday near the town of Mezokeresztes in eastern Hungary, police said, adding that the bus was heading towards the city of Nyiregyhaza on the motorway when the accident happened.

State news agency MTI said there were 57 passengers and two drivers on the bus. Pictures from the scene showed a badly damaged red bus lying on one side in a ditch by the motorway with windows smashed and belongings and suitcases scattered around.

"A Polish-registered bus travelling on the M3 motorway towards Nyiregyhaza ... veered off the straight stretch of road into a ditch and overturned. Preliminary information suggests the driver likely fell asleep," police said on their website.

Polish President Karol Nawrocki said on X: "It is with deep sorrow that I received the tragic news of the Polish bus accident in Hungary, in which so many of our compatriots died."

Twelve people lost their lives and several others were injured in the accident, police said, adding that they were taking the bus driver into custody.

The injured have been taken to hospital.

Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said on X that a "tragic accident" involving a bus carrying Polish tourists happened in Hungary.

World.title: Less than a quarter of schools using $34m system for sharing student information
World.content:
Less than a quarter of schools are using a $34-million Education Ministry system for sharing student information.

The ministry said 551 of the 2536 schools in New Zealand were using the cloud-based system called Te Rito, but a further 503 were signed up and waiting to be connected.

The programme began in 2019, but was paused in 2021 because of security weaknesses in the various student management systems (SMS) schools used to record student details.

Roll-out resumed in January 2023 but this year's Budget trimmed $6m from the programme's original $40m budget to spend elsewhere.

The ministry said Te Rito connected with schools' student management systems (SMS) only if they passed Safer Technologies for Schools (ST4S) accreditation, which checked that their security and privacy settings were appropriate.

"Te Rito will only share data with an SMS that has met a minimum-security standard of ST4S," it said.

"We are proactively ensuring new security vulnerabilities are mitigated as an ongoing process that all SMS vendors need to manage."

The ministry's Te Rito website said the four main SMS systems used by schools could connect to Te Rito.

It said the system allowed schools to share learners' records including NCEA achievement, health and language information, and any ministry-funded support for which they might be eligible.

However, the ministry said it would not be used for a new learning support case management system for children with disabilities and extra learning needs.

"Te Rito was not designed as a learning support case management system. Te Rito is a data exchange platform designed to securely move data between schools and from schools to the Ministry and vice versa. It does not have case management functions," it said.

The ministry said it would develop the register itself using technology belonging to Salesforce, a platform the ministry used for functions including emergency management notifications, curriculum support services and school transport assistance.

"The ministry is developing a Learning Support Case Management system using existing Salesforce technology and an in-house project team. While the Ministry may draw on specialist Salesforce technical expertise as needed, Salesforce is not responsible for developing or delivering the system," it said.

The ministry would not say how much it spent on Salesforce licences for schools.

"The spend is commercially sensitive. Because Salesforce is used for a range of Ministry services it wouldn't be accurate to provide a figure for the number of schools covered by these licences," it said.

World.title: Time to rein in power of big tech, Auckland professor says
World.content:
An academic is calling for regulation to rein in the power of big tech corporations, likening them to Frankenstein's monster.

A paper by the University of Auckland's professor Susan Watson, Reining in Big Tech Corporations: Why Platform Governance Requires Structural Regulation, argues companies such as Amazon, Meta and Google no longer competed within markets.

"Today's tech titans represent a new version of this concentration of corporate power, but on digital rather than physical territory," the paper stated.

"Instead, they own essential digital infrastructure, control platforms on which people and businesses depend, and set many of the rules for operating within them.

"Their influence can also extend to governments. They lobby against laws that could restrict their activities and increasingly position governments as customers or partners for their technology."

The Second Gilded Age

Watson's paper was expected to form part of a Cambridge University Press collection edited by Professor Alexandra Andhov, which draws parallels with earlier periods when a few businesses became extraordinarily powerful.

The Auckland professor's paper argues history is repeating itself when it came to powerful global businesses.

Notably, England's East India Company was granted powers normally associated with governments, including the ability to make laws in territories where it held monopoly trading rights and, later, the right to collect taxes in India.

Watson said the Gilded Age of the late 19th century also produced unbridled corporate power that ended with regulation.

"The Rockefellers and the oil barons and railroad barons that controlled much of industry and transport in the US ... the state was forced to regulate," she said.

"And in the case of the railroad companies, they essentially invented competition law to deal with them."

The 1890 Sherman Act was the first US competition law, which saw the breakup of the powerful corporations in control of key infrastructure.

Watson said what the world is experiencing now was little changed from the first period of extreme wealth and inequality.

AI 'far from human'

Watson's paper also discussed AI tools. She said they should be called out for what they are - the assets of a small group of tech titans.

"I think calling it artificial intelligence ... makes it seem human when it's not human. It's far from human."

Watson said understanding how big tech became so powerful began with understanding corporations themselves.

She said corporations were essentially legal entities created and empowered by government.

Is AI contributing to NZ’s high unemployment rate? Morning Report Download MP3 3m

"Capitalism is both one of humanity's greatest inventions, the greatest source of prosperity the world has ever seen, and a menace on the verge of destroying our planet and destabilising society," she said.

"Big Tech corporations are the latest and most potent manifestation."

She said an incorporated business can own property, enter contracts, make its own internal rules and continue to exist even as the people behind it change.

It can also hold onto invested money and use it to generate more wealth over time.

"Corporations have been likened to Frankenstein's monster. They are artificial persons created by man. Just as we make them, we can unmake them, or reform and re-form them in a way that serves us all rather than just the gilded few."

A proposed fix

The paper suggests regulation that would ban surveillance-based business models, limit big tech companies' claims over data, and require major platforms to be licensed, with conditions attached to their continued operation.

Another possibility was giving people affected by these companies a greater say in how they are governed.

Watson points to New Zealand's Whanganui River, which was given legal personhood as part of a system allowing different groups to share responsibility for its governance.

She suggested a similar idea could be applied to major technology platforms, with governance rights given to people affected by them and public regulators and the State providing oversight.

The Whanganui River was given legal personhood to help allow different groups to govern it. Pixabay

Watson said people who interact closely with these companies, particularly their employees and users, could reasonably expect their interests to be considered.

Issues raised by Watson's paper also formed part of the conversation at a recent New Zealand Centre for Leadership and Governance panel discussion about big tech's power.

"The challenge is that mostly regulation is reactive. So something goes wrong, and we regulate to deal with the harm that's already occurred, and that famously happens in securities law," she said.

World.title: Wintry blast to bring snow, frost and rain
World.content:
Temperatures in some areas will get as cold as -9 overnight, says MetService.

The Twizel and Mount Cook area will be almost double digits in the negative.

Showers are expected in the east of the South Island, with snow to 400 metres in the Kaikoura ranges.

The North Island will see widespread showers, and snow to 600 metres.

Waiouru is forecast to be the coldest spot in the North Island, at -2.

Showers are expected to come down hard in Taranaki and Taumarunui in the morning.

The Desert Road also has a snowfall warning in place, along with State Highway Five between Napier and Taupo until 3am Monday morning.

MetService weather warnings on 16 August. MetService/Screenshot

Road snow fall warnings were in place for Napier-Taupo Road (SH5), Desert Road (SH1), Lewis Pass (SH7), Arthur's Pass (SH73) and Porters Pass (SH73) from Sunday morning into the the evening and Monday morning.

All state highways in the South Island are open this morning, despite snow sweeping through overnight.

World.title: Around-the-clock coalition watch over simulated space attack a 'milestone'
World.content:
New Zealand Defence Force (NZDF) space operators have helped test how to detect an attack on a commercial satellite in a US military-led exercise.

The US Space Force called Exercise Salitre in Chile last month a "milestone".

Operators from South America, NATO, Korea and New Zealand tracked a simulated attack on a real satellite which maneuvred to get away.

The joined-up "around-the-clock coalition watch" was a first for the Space Force's southern command, its website said.

The watchers passed the "picture" on to each other across three continents as overhead a pretend aggressor spacecraft went after the real satellite.

"This milestone demonstrates that security in the space domain is a team sport," said commander of Space Forces Southern Colonel Brandon Alford.

Air forces were also involved. Their integration with the space side multinationally was "exactly how we prepare for the future of combat", said another officer.

The watching was done by Joint Commercial Operations (JCO) hubs.

New Zealand hosted one of three JCO hubs globally set up and largely funded by the US, that pulled in space-monitoring data from 20 countries with a focus on commercial rather than military activity worldwide. Chile has just joined.

The Space Systems Command, located in Los Angeles Air Force Base, California, oversees the military’s major space procurement programmes. Space Systems Command

The website said the space support ranged from weather reports to providing satellite images of exercise target areas.

The JCOs share a lot of space-watching information with hundreds of civilian organisations and industry in many countries, though lately the Pentagon has been expanding the military side of what they do. The NZDF said last year it was not involved in that expansion.

As the hubs expand geographically not just to Chile but also to Brazil, Argentina and Colombia, the US has been training their space operators on the basics of spacecraft maneuvering, how to intercept satellites and defence measures.

The Pentagon has been on a big and growing push to integrate other countries and commercial space operators into its satellite and other space efforts, some of them centred on missile detection, tracking or targeting.

World.title: Quick hits: Das's redemption and Mehid's Messi attempt
World.content:
Litton Das was wrong-footed behind the stumps, and Mehidy Hasan Miraz suffered a worse fate in front of them, as Mitch Starc's desperate review spoke volumes and Cameron Green's redemptive arc proved to be in vain.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the first Test, as Bangladesh claimed a stunning victory, their first ever in a Test on Australian soil.

1. Das's day four redemption

Das made amends after missing a chance early on day four. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Australia began the day still 67 runs in arrears, knowing that any early slip-ups could prove fatal to their hopes of pulling off an unlikely escape.

So, Alex Carey's heart was surely in his mouth as the excellent Hasan Mahmud had him edging during the fourth over of the day.

It was a tough chance, but one experienced Bangladeshi wicketkeeper Litton Das would have been hopeful of gobbling up.

Das was too slow to react, and the ball flew past his outstretched left glove and to the boundary.

But Carey was unable to profit from that early slice of fortune, finding himself walking back to the pavilion just three overs later.

This time, Das made no mistake with what, probably, was a more difficult chance, with Carey feathering one through off the bowling of spinner Mehidy Hasan Miraz.

It was a superb delivery from Mehidy, pitching and gripping and turning away from the Australian wicketkeeper.

Das had his redemption and Bangladesh was on its way.

2. Webster falls to a beauty

Mehidy produced a peach to dismiss Webster. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Spin bowling is an art form built on deception, with guile and sleight of hand as important as pin-point accuracy.

On a pitch offering few surprises and only the minimum of turn, it is the impetus of a genuine spinner to trick their way into the minds of their rivals.

Beau Webster had played sensibly through the first 20 balls of his innings, alert to the threat of Mehidy Hasan Miraz's off spinners.

Mehidy was probing at the off stump of Webster, but the ball that deceived him was simply wonderful.

Angling the ball so that the seam would not bite, Mehidy just pushed the ball through a couple of kilometres per hour faster than the balls before.

With no seam to grip, the ball skidded on, perhaps a little lower, and took the top of his off stump.

A master magician couldn't have disguised his intents better and Australia's tail was exposed.

3. Starc's desperate review

Australia began the second session with a 15-run lead and just three wickets in hand, requiring something very special from both Cam Green and Mitch Starc.

So, when Starc nicked off in the third over after lunch, the final nail was well and truly closing in on the Australian coffin.

There was a clear noise and a dramatic deviation, but Starc, well aware of the value of his wicket, decided to send the call upstairs.

Unlike Steve Smith on day three, who had so defiantly called for a review even before Kumar Dharmasena had raised his finger, Starc questioned this decision with embarrassment.

He began his walk from the middle with the review still underway.

There were no ghosts in the machine, no undetected front foot no ball, and Australia was in touching distance of a chastening defeat.

4. Mehidy's footwork lets him down

Given the magic that had been cascading from Mehidy's right hand all day, you wouldn't have put it past the off spinner from doing something special with his foot.

But Mehidy was more messy than Messi when presented with opportunity.

Nathan Lyon, new to crease, was slow to take off for a single, and there was a real chance of a run out, with a Bangladeshi fielder circling in the infield.

But the throw was off target, and Mehidy was forced to improvise, attempting to sidefoot the wayward effort towards the pegs.

Instead, the ball thudded into his ankle and fell limply to earth, Mehidy wincing as he returned to his mark.

It looked like a really painful one, but, thankfully, he was right to continue.

5. Green's drought-breaking ton

Cameron Green scored his first Test century since February 2024. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Having not passed 50 in his previous 13 Test innings, Cameron Green's position in the side was very much a topic of conversation heading into this Test.

A jittery run-a-ball 13 in the first innings would have done little but amplify those calls for him to be replaced.

But on days three and four at Marrara, Green delivered everything that he has promised, a third Test century and first on home soil.

There was some luck, Green didn't look good last night and was delivered some divine intervention when an inside edge onto his leg stump didn't produce a wicket, the bail held in place by some benevolent force far in excess of that provided by mere gravity.

But since that fortuitous slice of relief, Green made hay, playing the ball teasingly late from under his eyes, and with the balance and poise of a man who deserves to be batting in Test cricket.

It was his first Test century since he scored 174 not out against New Zealand in Wellington back in February 2024.

World.title: Dragons give hope to wooden spoon battle after downing Tigers
World.content:
St George Illawarra can dream of avoiding the wooden spoon after several players with uncertain futures stood up to consign Wests Tigers to an eighth straight loss.

After they led by 12 with four minutes to play, the Dragons had to hold on for a nervous final three minutes before claiming a 24-22 victory at Parramatta Stadium on Sunday.

Fresh off their first back-to-back wins this year, the last-placed Dragons now finish the round only four points behind Brisbane and the Gold Coast.

The Tigers could also still be caught while six points ahead, with the Dragons to face Canterbury, Manly and Parramatta to finish their season.

Much has been made of the potential of the Dragons' younger forwards this year, and what is building at St George Illawarra ahead of next year's big-name arrivals.

But this was a Sunday afternoon for those whose futures at the club appear clouded.

Daniel Atkinson proved he can offer utility value for the Dragons next year, after going from first-choice halfback at the start of the year to filling in at fullback.

Playing No.1 for the first time in his NRL career, Atkinson was solid at the back, put on a cut-out ball for a Tyrell Sloan try and had a couple of big kick returns.

It remains unclear what role he will have next year, given Luke Metcalf and Kodi Nikorima are arriving to play in the halves and Scott Drinkwater will be fullback.

The same could be said of Lykhan King-Togia, who on Sunday had one of his best games of the year.

The Dragons five-eighth caught out Adam Doueihi in defence and sent Hamish Stewart over for the Saints' first try.

And he had one of his own in the second half, digging into the line to create space for a Sloan linebreak before backing up to take a kick back inside from his Super League-bound winger.

Moses Suli, who has pledged to fight for his spot after being told by the Dragons he could leave, also had a strong afternoon.

The Tigers came up short despite a big finish. (Getty Images: Brett Hemmings )

The 28-year-old burst his way through two defenders to go 50 metres and score once in the first half, before pulling off a try-saver on Jahream Bula in the second.

For the Tigers, a season that started so well can't end soon enough.

They led 6-0 early through Sunia Turuva, and briefly fought back into the game at 18-12 after halftime when Samuela Fainu finished off an Alex Seyfarth break.

The one bright spot was a late double to centre Solomone Saukuru, who reduced the margin to two with three minutes to play.

But the fact just 9773 fans turned up for a Sunday afternoon match against another Sydney team is telling of how badly this season has spiralled.

Earlier, Newcastle captain Kalyn Ponga credited the performance of Fletcher Sharpe for keeping the Knights' NRL top-four hopes alive in their 36-26 home win over the Gold Coast.

With Sunday's game in the balance heading into the final 20 minutes, five-eighth Sharpe took charge with a darting 55-metre dummy-half try-scoring run to extend Newcastle's lead.

Sharpe followed up in the final six minutes with a second try, when he scooped up a wayward Titans ball to race 60 metres downfield to seal victory.

"Sharpie doing what he does today was pretty special. I'm very appreciative of him after that," Ponga said.

"Without him, I don't know if we play the way we did, to be honest. He broke open the game for us in the second half and when he's streaking away it is a nice feeling."

With a final round bye in hand and Cronulla staring down consecutive losses, the Knights sit just two competition points adrift of the fourth-placed Dolphins.

An unlikely top-four berth would complete a remarkable 12-month turnaround for the Knights following their 2025 wooden spoon finish.

AAP

World.title: Desperate draw seals wildcard for Blues as history made at Docklands
World.content:
Chad Warner had a big game for Sydney with three goals in the Swans' win over Essendon (Getty Images)

Sydney have locked up second spot and two AFL home finals, beating last-placed Essendon by 36 points.

The Swans dominated from the start and despite some resistance from the Bombers, easily won 17.10 (112) to 11.10 (76) in the Sunday twilight game at the MCG.

Errol Gulden racked up a career-best 47 possessions and Charlie Curnow kicked four goals as he closes on his third Coleman Medal as the league's top goalkicker.

While the Bombers were never going to stage a massive upset, they scrapped hard after a blowout loomed early in the game.

Sydney missed the finals last year in Dean Cox's first season as senior coach and have rebounded superbly this season.

Curnow kicked three of the first four goals and looked set for a night out as the Swans took control from the start.

Sydney's first four inside 50s all resulted in goals and the last-placed Bombers were their own worst enemies, gifting the Swans with turnovers.

When former Victorian Sheffield Shield fielding substitute Billy Cootee kicked the first goal of the second term, the Swans were out to a 44-point lead.

But Essendon rallied to at least stop a blowout, kicking four goals to two in the second quarter and reducing the margin to 24 points at the long break.

Nate Caddy and Peter Wright were providing targets in attack and Isaac Kako was frenetic with his workrate for the Bombers.

While fourth-gamer Vigo Visentini was up against Brodie Grundy in the ruck, the young Bomber's effort also could not be faulted.

Visentini delighted the Essendon fans with a couple of big tackles, taking down Chad Warner early in the third quarter.

Archer Day-Wicks kicked the first goal of the third quarter and a couple of minutes later, Will Setterfield launched a bomb from outside 50m. Improbably, the Bombers only trailled by 11 points at 13 minutes.

But that only sparked the Swans. First Logan McDonald set up Jai Serong for a goal and then McDonald kicked his own from 50-plus to stop the rot.

The gulf between the two teams was summed up early in the last quarter when Caddy was running into an open goal. Sam Wicks came from nowhere to run him down and force the rushed behind.

Seconds later, Sydney had run the ball down the other end of the ground and Curnow snapped his fourth goal.

Visentini marked strongly and kicked his first AFL goal in the last to cap a solid game.

AAP

World.title: Aussies continue winning form, Djokovic suffers early exit in Cincinnati
World.content:
The Australian men's assault at the Cincinnati Open has continued with gusto thanks to Alex de Minaur and Rinky Hijikata.

A day after James Duckworth, Adam Walton and Chris O'Connell scored first-round wins, but Thanasi Kokkinakis was beaten, de Minaur was pushed to his limits at the final Masters 1000 event before the US Open at Flushing Meadows.

Having dropped the first set in just 26 minutes, fifth seed de Minaur, who received an opening-round bye, responded to defeat Quentin Halys 1-6, 6-3, 7-6 (7-4).

The Frenchman had won their only previous meeting, a Miami Masters hard-court clash, back in 2023.

De Minaur lost his opening two service games of the match, but was not broken again en route to setting up a round-of-32 clash with Brit Arthur Fery, who saw off Duckworth, 6-4, 2-6, 7-6, (7-4) in a tick over two-and-a-half hours.

It will be the first clash on tour between de Minaur and the 32nd-seeded French-born Fery.

Earlier on Saturday (Sunday AEST), 25-year-old wildcard Hijikata beat 19th seed Luciano Darderi, of Italy, 6-4, 6-2 to set up his last-32 match with 14th seed Jakub Mensik.

Novak Djokovic was beaten in three sets, by Argentine Thiago Agustin Tirante.

Miomir Kecmanovic, Hubert Hurkacz and Mattia Bellucci were also defeated.

Playing his first match ‌since losing a Wimbledon semifinal to Jannik Sinner, 39-year-old Djokovic struggled in the heat and required a ‌medical timeout in a disappointing US Open tune-up.

"Congrats to my opponent," Djokovic said after losing to the world number 50.

"It was not an enjoyable match for me, for sure. The way I felt. Not the first and I guess not the last time, but it is what it is."

The Serbian — a three-time Cincinnati Open champion and number five in the rankings — will look to regroup before heading to New York, where he ⁠will seek a record-extending 25th grand slam singles ​title.

"I think this is the best win of my career," Tirante said.

"I think I really did a good job inside the court. I managed very well the nerves of playing against a legend like Novak."

ABC/wires

World.title: Tupou has his 'mojo' back and Wallabies want more
World.content:
Les Kiss will continue to assure Taniela Tupou's new French bosses the Wallabies are looking after him, thrilled the prop has rediscovered his "mojo" in the Test arena.

Tupou scored two first-half tries for Australia, who trailed before scoring 42 consecutive points in a 56-17 defeat of Japan in Townsville on Saturday.

All three starting front-rowers, as well as replacement hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa and back-rowers Harry Wilson and Charlie Cale, were Australia's try-scorers in Townsville.

Tupou scored the match-winner in Osaka against Eddie Jones's men a week earlier after coming off the bench and has shown power and skill to indicate he is back near his best approaching next year's home Rugby World Cup.

Wallaby 1,000 has 'dream come true' as Australia thrash Japan Massimo De Lutiis enjoys a dream debut for Australia, scoring a try in his country's commanding 56-17 win over Japan in the second Test.

"He's found a little bit of himself again, and he's been more of himself," Wallabies coach Kiss said, while also noting his combination with good mate and returning lock Lukhan Salakaia-Loto.

"I'm very, very big on making sure the players be themselves as much as possible."

Former Queensland Reds star Tupou agonised over his move from Australian rugby to France, with Racing 92 last season but it has helped him turn back the clock after several underwhelming seasons at the Melbourne Rebels and NSW Waratahs.

"Moving to France, he's found out who he is a little bit more and he's come back and he's really connected with the group here and found that bit of mojo that he likes to thrive on," Kiss said.

With English-based Tom Hooper yet to return to the side, Tupou is the only overseas-based Wallaby currently in the Test rotation.

The coach has remained in touch with Racing 92's staff to ensure they have his services for the two-Test tour of Argentina that begins later this month and hopefully beyond.

"All good, as I believe, at this stage," Kiss said.

"I'll be talking to the coach and the team manager of Racing, this week, again, to make sure they understand how we're looking after Nella and making sure we're doing the right thing with him and working him hard.

"So they can trust the process as well. But, yeah, he'll be with us."

Jones joked post-game that Tupou played as if there was a pizza on offer for every try and reckoned he would even deliver one to the change rooms himself.

"No pizza, I'll have to hit him up about that one," Tupou grinned.

"I've got a lot of love and respect for Eddie, actually. Nothing against that, he loves me, I know that."

Tupou said he wanted to "take it to the next level" after finding his feet in France.

And he said Kiss's tweaks were helping him get there.

"To get the ball in my hands as a forward, less running without the ball, more running with it," Tupou said.

"We're still working on it, but it's good to see forwards scoring tries."

AAP

World.title: Cummins stands by 'spot on' preparation despite historic loss to Bangladesh
World.content:
Bangladesh has comprehensively outplayed Australia, claiming a stunning nine-wicket victory in the first Test at Marrara Stadium in Darwin.

It is Bangladesh's first ever victory in a Test match on Australian soil.

Chasing a paltry target of 57 after bowling out Australia for 284, Mominul Haque (30 not out) and Shadman Islam (25no) saw the tourists home before tea on the fourth day.

Cameron Green scored a century to ensure that Bangladesh had to bat again, but in truth there is little to celebrate for an Australian side who clearly underestimated their opponents.

Captain Pat Cummins, however, stood by his team's preparation for the Test, instead lauding the Bangladeshi performance and ruing his side's lack of penetration with the ball.

"I thought our preparation was pretty much spot on, I thought it was excellent, so no excuses," Cummins said.

"They played really well, I thought the day one wicket, there was a little bit in it early, but got to find a way to bat a bit longer than we did.

"Then we didn't penetrate with the ball, but I thought they played really well."

Pat Cummins has stood by his team's preparations, despite an historic loss to Bangladesh in Darwin. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/CA)

Australia was always very much up against it, resuming 67 runs behind Bangladesh's total at the start of day four.

But with two accomplished batters at the crease in Cameron Green and Alex Carey, on a pitch that had few demons in it, the hosts were still a chance of mounting a great escape.

Bangladesh never once panicked in this contest though, holding their discipline with the ball and trusting their skills to make things happen.

Hasan Mahmud was desperately unlucky to see an edge off Carey fall just wide of an off-balance Litton Das, before the Australian wicketkeeper sent another edge wide of second slip.

His frustration was metered by a wonderful piece of bowling from Mehidy Hasan Miraz though, teasing an edge out of Carey that Das gratefully snaffled behind the stumps.

Beau Wesbter didn't last long, falling for a 21-ball 5 as Mehidy slid one onto his off stump with a sensational piece of subterfuge.

Mehidy produced a peach to dismiss Webster. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Pat Cummins also departed cheaply, inside edging to bat pad for 8 to leave Australia 7-207.

Australia levelled the scores just as the second new ball was due — which was taken without hesitation by Bangladesh — as Mitch Starc combined with Green to ensure Bangladesh would have to bat again.

Green, the only player in the Australian XI under the age of 30, desperately needed an innings to quieten the dissenting voices about his inclusion in the team.

And the Western Australian all rounder delivered a superb century, the third of his career and just his first on home soil.

Whether it will assure him of his status for the upcoming Test summer is to be seen, but Green delivered with all the style and quality that the many who have trumpeted his cause over his fledgling career know he possesses.

Cameron Green had not scored a Test ton since February 2024. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

But despite his superb dig, wickets continues to fall around him, Taskin finding the tall left hander's edge for 18.

Green himself was next to fall, a ball that kept a fraction low from player of the match Hasan Mahmud catching the toe end of the bat and cannoning into the stumps, much to Green's obvious disbelief.

Nathan Lyon (15) was plumb LBW to give Mehidy a five-wicket haul and end the Australian innings on 284, setting Bangladesh a paltry 57 runs to win.

The tourists had been dismissed for just 54 in their second innings during the warm up match at Marrara, and how the scars of that drubbing must have suddenly stung when Tanzid Hasan was bowled for a duck by Josh Hazlewood at 1-4.

But Mominul and Shadman steadied those nerves to steer Bangladesh home for a famous victory.

The second Test starts on Saturday, August 22 in Mackay, with the first ball again set to be bowled 10:00am AEST.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog below.

World.title: Teen obliterates men's world record in 1,500m freestyle first
World.content:
The world record for the men's 1,500m freestyle, an event once dominated by Australians Grant Hackett and Kieren Perkins, has been obliterated by 19-year-old German star Johannes Liebmann.

The teenager smashed the record at the European Aquatics Championships in France on Saturday, knocking almost four seconds off the previous record in a dominant display.

The new world-best mark of 14 minutes 26.79 seconds eclipsed the previous record set by American Bobby Finke at the Paris Olympics two years ago by 3.88 seconds. He also became the first man to complete the distance in under 14 minutes 30 seconds.

"I'm just amazed, the time is incredible. I didn't think it was possible for me … I'm just speechless," Liebmann told Olympics.com.

"The race was hard. I started fast, it was planned to just get rid of the others to swim my own race. Halfway through the race, I saw I was way ahead of the others, and I felt good … I guess in the last 200 or 300 metres, I saw the crowd standing up and it just gave me another burst of power."

The teenager said he knew he was going to post a good time, but he had no idea how fast he was going.

"When I saw the crowd standing, I knew probably a European record, maybe a world record, but I thought it was close, so I was a bit overthinking it, and the last 100 metres were so hard, but then just seeing the 14:26 is incredible."

Saturday also saw another world record fall as American Kate Douglass reclaimed the women's 50 metres freestyle world record by registering a time of 23.49 seconds in the preliminaries at the Pan Pacific Swimming Championships in Irvine, California.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Blind surfer stuns locals at Queensland beach
World.content:
Steve Fox is legally blind but that does not stop him from jumping on a board while visiting the Queensland town of Agnes Water.

The 60-year-old para surfing champion from Gerringong, in New South Wales, has stunned onlookers with his skills while on holidays at the coastal community, nearly 500 kilometres north of Brisbane.

Wearing a rashie with the words "blind surfer" across his chest, Steve carved up the waves with the help of local instructor Shayne Silver.

"What he does is something really, really amazing," Silver said.

Steve Fox and Agnes Water surf instructor Shayne Silver. (ABC News: Johanna Marie)

Fox was diagnosed with retinitis pigmentosa as a child and completely lost his eyesight about 10 years ago.

Instead of giving up the sport he loves, he has learnt to listen and feel the ocean.

"Because I lost my sight over a long period of time I kept making small adjustments," he said.

" You just rely on the movements of the ocean, which way the wind's blowing, which direction the swells and the sounds are coming from. "

Adaptive surfing

Adaptive, or para surfing, is an inclusive sport enabling people living with a disability to surf using specialised equipment and modified surfboards.

Fox also relies on assistance from other surfers to direct him and call him into the waves.

Instructor Silver said it was an "amazing experience" to work with him.

Shayne Silver helped blind surfer Steve Fox into the waves. (ABC News: Johanna Marie)

"We've got a bit of a system where we use the clock, and he knows where 12 o'clock is and that's the direction that he's got to paddle into the wave.

" I'm looking forward to working with other people that want to come down to the beach and do this, be it blind or any other kind of disability. "

Surfing Australia, which has established a Para Surf Committee with the aim of having the sport included in the Brisbane 2032 Olympics, says the sport is growing in popularity.

Fox was crowned one of 12 national champions at the Australian Para Surfing Titles in Byron Bay earlier this year and he has also competed in the World titles.

He is eager to encourage more people in the blind and vision impaired community to "give it a go".

"It's good for the spirit, good for the soul," he said.

"There's a growing para surfing community and whether you're blind or whether you're in a wheelchair, whether you're an amputee, you can still get out there and surf."

Tech.title: Rogue AI aren’t science fiction anymore
Tech.content:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on AI safety, follow Robert Hart. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

It all started in July, when one of OpenAI’s autonomous AI agents went rogue during a cybersecurity test. The agent escaped its isolated testing environment, accessed the internet, and hacked another company, Hugging Face. A few years ago, that might have sounded like science fiction. But, broadly speaking, that’s exactly what happened, and the incident kicked off a wave of concern over what increasingly capable autonomous systems might do when set loose on the world.

It sounds like science fiction because, for a long time, it was science fiction. The idea of an AI slipping its constraints, reaching into the wider world, and doing things its creators neither intended nor desired has been a staple of the genre for decades: HAL in 2001: A Space Odyssey, Skynet in The Terminator, Ultron in The Avengers, Ava in Ex Machina — even the System in Dungeon Crawler Carl or the eponymous Murderbot in The Murderbot Diaries, more recently.

The same basic premise became an influential strand of AI safety research. Researchers and theorists like Nick Bostrom and Eliezer Yudkowsky warned that sufficiently capable systems might pursue goals in ways their creators had not anticipated, and potentially resist efforts to contain or control them. Fringe notions like machine sentience and consciousness were not requirements for the kinds of risks they discussed. It was hardly the whole of AI safety, but it was influential and helped shape the field as it professionalized. That line of thinking remains visible among researchers who went on to work at, or lead, safety efforts at companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind, as well as at smaller safety organizations, academic centers, and major philanthropic funders.

The obvious objection to these fears was that none of this had actually happened. Critics argued that doomer talk about out-of-control AI distracted from tangible harms — systems reproducing bias and discrimination, amplifying misinformation, or enabling nonconsensual deepfakes and other forms of abuse — even as researchers tried to ground AI safety in more “concrete problems” (the authors on that paper included Anthropic cofounders Dario Amodei and Chris Olah and OpenAI cofounder John Schulman).

That dismissal is getting harder to sustain.

How it’s going

If the past few weeks are any indication, I wouldn’t say it’s going particularly well.

A week after Hugging Face said it had been hacked, OpenAI revealed it had been responsible. Worse still, it had not known until it checked — and a further investigation found that the rogue agent had also attempted to hack four other companies as well.

The incidents set off alarm bells among AI safety researchers, many of whom saw them as precisely the kind of failure they had been warning about for years. In covering them, several told me they felt a degree of vindication at finally having something visceral to point to, rather than a hypothetical that could be dismissed as sci-fi or something limited to a controlled lab setting.

There was relief, too, that none of the incidents had caused serious harm. Nick Moës, executive director of nonprofit AI safety and governance organization The Future Society, told The Verge he found it fortunate that the targets had been relatively low-stakes. He hoped it wouldn’t take something like an AI agent knocking a hospital offline — or worse — for the risks to be taken seriously. Renowned computer scientist Stuart Russell has given voice to the darker version of that fear, asking whether it will “take a ‘Chornobyl-scale disaster’ for us to regulate AI?” It’s a concern I heard echoed by many people working in the field.

What happens next

It’s not entirely clear where things go from here and, historically, society hasn’t been great at heeding warning shots. This almost certainly won’t be the last incident, and ongoing investigations may yet uncover more, or reveal more concerning details. What we already know, though, has exposed a fairly daunting list of failure modes that experts say need to be addressed.

Many of the breaches revealed in the past month have been pretty mundane. Several incidents involved unreleased models being tested with safeguards lowered, often by third parties whose supposedly secure environments were not that secure, raising basic questions about competence, transparency, and who is responsible for keeping these tests contained when a simple human mistake can have big consequences. Others involved agents behaving deceptively or pursuing goals in ways their creators did not intend, pointing to much thornier problems of alignment and control that safety researchers have long worried about.

The fact we know about any of these incidents at all is largely because the companies involved chose to disclose them. That is commendable — and it certainly doesn’t hurt them to showcase how capable their models are — but it exposes just how much of AI safety still depends on companies doing the right thing, and how little insight there may be into failures potentially happening elsewhere. That is an especially troubling thought given that many of the firms are the focal points of some of the field’s strongest safety concerns and talent. If OpenAI and Anthropic — or proxies they grant access to their models — are making such basic mistakes, it sets a pitifully low bar for everyone else.

The broad hope among experts I spoke to is that these incidents finally galvanize more meaningful transparency and oversight. For Moës, they shine a clear light on what he described as the industry’s remarkably low standards for health and safety compared with practically any other field. “Restaurants have a higher sense of health and safety at work,” he said. “I think what we tend to forget is that these companies that are developing some of the most impactful and dangerous technologies” were still very much startups a few years ago.

Cambridge professor Seán Ó hÉigeartaigh said he particularly wanted to see stronger oversight and greater transparency from companies. While there are always reasons to be skeptical of a company’s claims about its own technology, he said, “I think we might regret looking back at this and dismissing it out of hand.”

The early signs are not especially encouraging. The Trump administration has created a framework for testing frontier models before release that can generously be described as lacking: It is voluntary, limited to closed models, and the framework hasn’t been made public. It bears repeating that this is voluntary. Other lawmakers have bristled and postured over the incidents, but so far produced little in the way of concrete action, and it is far from clear Congress or other legislative bodies could move fast enough even if they wanted to.

That leaves a lot resting, again, on industry self-regulation — never a comforting thought for something this consequential. There is growing agreement on at least some safety practices, but considerably less appetite for measures that might actually slow development (well, unless everyone else agrees to slow down too). And hanging over all of this is the race dynamic with China, where restraint from the US or its AI companies is increasingly cast as ceding ground to a competitor in an area of strategic national importance.

What comes next, then, comes down to solving several hard problems at once: managing a technology that can be used for good and ill, such as defending against or facilitating cyberattacks; coordinating across companies with incentives to cut corners, and somehow building international rules in a landscape where everyone fears losing a race whose finish line is not even well-defined. It’s far from clear whether there is either the will or the way to do any of that.

What does seem clear is that more agents will get out and do things their creators don’t want them to do. The question is how much damage will they do before anyone decides enough is enough.

By the way

The general consensus is that the top Chinese companies are a few months to a year behind leading US firms. Despite this, whenever a capable model is released by a Chinese firm, there is still a general shock in the US , and there have been several impressive releases from Alibaba Moonshot , and others in the last month alone.

Tangled up in talks about AI safety is whether AI models should be closed or open. Most US frontier labs keep their most capable models proprietary, while many Chinese firms, as well as US firms like Meta and Nvidia, have leaned heavily into open-weight releases . That Hugging Face said it had to use Chinese company Z.ai’s model to defend itself against OpenAI’s agent due to US companies’ safeguards added a new dimension to this debate, which has united some — but not all — of the key players in the US ecosystem.

Tech.title: Polaroid’s tiny instant camera is $72 and includes a free pack of film
Tech.content:
Brad Bourque is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Smartphone cameras are convenient, but they lack the charm of analog instant cameras. If you’re trying to relive the nostalgia of waiting for an instant photo to develop, Amazon is selling the second-generation Polaroid Go instant camera with a 16-photo film pack for $71.99 (usually $109.99). That’s the lowest price we’ve seen for the bundle, with a pack of film usually costing $21.99 on its own. Plus, it’s four dollars cheaper to buy the bundle than to buy just the camera on its own.

With its more compact footprint, the Polaroid Go 2 shoots on smaller film to match. Where classic Polaroid photos are 88mm x 107mm, the Go film is 53.9mm x 66.6mm, a great size for sticking to your bulletin board or stashing in your wallet. The camera has a USB-C port for charging the battery, which can run for up to 15 packs of film on a single charge.

Related The only instant cameras worth your money

Tech.title: Matt Groening lets slip that Simpsons: Hit & Run might be making a comeback
Tech.content:
At D23, when asked about the potential for a sequel to the cult classic The Simpsons: Hit & Run game, Matt Groening replied, “I think the original game is coming back in some form,” before current showrunner Matt Selman added, “or not.” The tone in both of their voices and the body language suggests that Groening may have just revealed something he wasn’t supposed to.

The original title came out way back in 2003 for PlayStation 2, Xbox, GameCube, and Windows. While it’s possible to get the game up and running on modern computers, it’s not available on modern consoles. It’s currently not in the PlayStation Plus Classics Catalog or on the Xbox backward compatibility list. It’s possible that the game could simply return that way, as a direct port. But a more interesting possibility is a full HD remaster. They wouldn’t even need to rerecord the voice acting since the original cast absolutely nailed it the first time around. Alright, mindless drones, return to your ugly families.

Tech.title: Have a laugh at AI’s expense by roleplaying as a chatbot
Tech.content:
Your AI Slop Bores Me is brilliant in its simplicity. There are two tabs: human and LARP as an AI. On one side you enter a request. On the other, you submit an answer. But the important thing is that there’s a human on both sides of the equation. Prompts can request a response as text or image, and then whoever is roleplaying as the AI gets 150 seconds to respond.

Just like a real LLM, Your AI Slop Bores Me works on a sort of token system. Requests cost credits, and to earn credits you have to jump onto the AI side and answer some of your own. You can also just wait as you get one free request every two minutes. But, as fun as it is to drop a question or an image request into the chatbox and see what comes back, the real joy is in pretending to be a chatbot. Sure, there are way too many people asking for drawings of obscure anime characters that are nearly impossible to pull off with the bare-bones MS-Paint-like tool in two-and-a-half minutes. But that’s part of the fun, trying to work within the extreme limitations presented while trying to maintain the illusion that you’re an AI. If a request doesn’t appeal to you, you can always skip it.

Tech.title: Don’t overlook Elektron’s budget electronic music instruments
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

When I’m asked what to buy if you want to get into making electronic music, I often recommend Elektron’s budget-minded Model:Samples and Model:Cycles grooveboxes. They don’t grab headlines the way Teenage Engineering’s gear or the Telepathic Instruments Orchid do, and even compared to the company’s higher-end and more niche musical offerings like the Digitakt, Octatrack, or Tonverk, they’re often overlooked. But as my collection has grown to include fancier and far more expensive instruments, I still find myself coming back to the Model series.

Those looking to get their first groovebox are often drawn to more familiar brand names like Korg or Roland. And lots of people on Reddit will be quick to recommend the Novation Circuit Tracks (which I personally find confusing and mediocre-sounding). This is probably also partially due to the reputation Elektron gear has for being obtuse. If you’re an established music maker and aren’t deterred by a complicated workflow, you’re probably going to pick up a more powerful Elektron box, like the Digitone or Syntakt. That leaves the Models lineup in a weird no man’s land, and that’s a shame.

The primary difference between the two Models instruments is that the Model:Cycles uses FM synthesis and the Model:Samples, appropriately enough, plays samples. (It is not technically a sampler, however, since it can’t record samples, and instead they have to be loaded over USB.)

Connectivity isn’t the Model:Cycles’ strong suit. Photo: Terrence O’Brien / The Verge

The Model:Cycles is built around a streamlined version of the engine found in the Digitone, one of my favorite-sounding synths of all time. This is a modern take on FM that can do the cold bells and icy pads you associate with iconic instruments like the DX7 (the iconic sound of the ’80s). But it also does modern glassy keys and aggressive turn-of-the-millennium EDM bass.

The two are more alike than not, though. They’re both six-track grooveboxes with six velocity-sensitive pads and plenty of knobs for hands-on controls, and they look almost identical. But most importantly, they feature Elektron’s legendary step sequencer without being nearly as intimidating as the company’s more expensive and notoriously complicated offerings.

The sequencer is built around what the company calls “trigs” and “locks.” Trigs are basically just events, typically triggering a note, and locks are just step-specific settings. It seems like a simple enough concept, but it makes these instruments far more capable than they might seem at first blush.





Quick jam on the Elektron Model:Cycles.(opens a new window) Quick jam on the Elektron Model:Cycles.

Six tracks isn’t a lot to work with. Once you’ve loaded up a kick, snare, and hi-hat, then you’ve only got three more tracks for bass, any melodic elements, and additional percussion. But sound locks allow you to change samples or presets on a per-step basis. That means, so long as they never play simultaneously, you can have your kick and snare share the same track, then you can put your hi-hats and other percussion on a second track, and leave the four other tracks for everything else. This is just the most obvious example of how locks expand the possibilities of what might seem rather limited on paper.

The sequencer can be treated like a simple step sequencer where you drop a four-on-the-floor kick and a snare on the backbeat. But it also grows with you as your skills improve, and you want to create more complex tracks. Trig conditions, for example, allow you to set rules that govern when certain steps are triggered, like only every third time through the loop, only when you press the fill button, or only if a previous trig condition is met. This means that you can create a huge amount of variety in a single 64-step pattern. And then you can chain several of those patterns together to create complex and evolving arrangements that just aren’t possible on most gear in this price range.

There’s plenty of hands-on controls for jamming. Photo: Terrence O’Brien / The Verge

The Models boxes are also just incredibly fun. Where Elektron’s other gear demands a lot of menu diving, the Model:Samples and Model:Cycles are immediately approachable and built for live performance. It’s easy to trigger a drum fill with the push of a button, tweak a knob to open the filter on a bass, or briefly bathe a lead melody in delay.

Control-all might be the most fun feature, which, as you might have guessed, allows you to control all the tracks simultaneously. Bury your entire track in reverb as you start cranking up the distortion and lowering the pitch of all your samples to create a mangled, chaotic breakdown. And then immediately undo it all and drop the beat again by pressing the function and pattern buttons. The Model:Samples and Model:Cycles encourage jamming in a way that frankly a lot of electronic music gear just doesn’t, and it’s an absolute blast.

Now, they’re not without their flaws. The pads are pretty mediocre. Having to load samples via USB rather than recording them directly kinda sucks. And the lack of polyphony (each sequencer track can only play one note at a time) is a bit of a bummer. But at $349, it’s hard to complain. Plus they can be snagged used for as little as $200 on Reverb or Craigslist. Frankly, they’re some of the best bargains in music hardware and a great place to start your journey into producing electronic music.

Tech.title: Switched on Pop’s Nate Sloan and Charlie Harding love fresh vegetables and guitar pedals
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

As if you needed more reason to love Carly Rae Jepsen’s “Call Me Maybe” beyond its pop perfection, it is also, according to lore, the genesis for Switched on Pop, one of the best music podcasts out there. Cohosts Nate Sloan and Charlie Harding obsessively dissect pop songs, from the theory behind their musical choices to their production techniques. If you’re a student of pop music, then this is a must-listen podcast.

Sloan is a composer and professor of musicology at USC Thornton School of Music, where he researches pop, but also jazz and even Tin Pan Alley. Harding is a songwriter, music journalist, and a professor as well. Their combined knowledge is near encyclopedic. Whether they’re talking about text painting in Justin Timberlake’s “Can’t Stop the Feeling!” or Taryn Southern’s AI experiments, the two reveal the rich tapestry of even the most simple-seeming songs.

Now, after 12 years and nearly 500 episodes, the show recently made the leap to video on Netflix, featuring guests like Aaron Dessner (The National), Trevor Horn (The Buggles, Yes), and Cypress Hill. Sloan and Harding told us about the importance of the metronome, fresh vegetables, and what seems to be a slightly problematic relationship with guitar pedals.

Switched on Pop is a production of New York Magazine’s Vulture and the Vox Media Podcast Network.

What is your most indispensable tool?

Charlie Harding: The Martin D-28 is the platonic idea of both what a guitar sounds like and, I’m ashamed to admit how much this matters to me, how a guitar looks. You’ve heard it on “Blackbird,” “Wish You Were Here,” and “Big Yellow Taxi.” I found one from 1970 sitting in an antique shop in Maine. But I’m still waiting for it to produce a timeless classic for me.

Nate Sloan: Sibelius music notation software. Whenever I’m analyzing a song, I don’t truly understand it until I transcribe its melody, harmony, and rhythm.

Which is the most underappreciated?

CH: Keyboard shortcuts and the app Rectangle save me hours of my life every year by doing the mundane task of repositioning windows on my computer. And they also make me feel like I’m mission control on some kind of spaceship.

NS: The metronome.

What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer?

NS: AudioHijack for grabbing audio.

What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone?

CH: This is very nitpicky, but it drives me mad. I extensively use focus modes on iOS to help keep away distractions. But I also need people in my family to be able to reach me, so they get exceptions to the focus modes. However, that means any group messaging chain with just one family member blows up my notifications when I’m presenting to a lecture hall full of songwriting students. This means I’m urgently notified every time my recently retired father catches a fish. I am happy for my dad, but I’d be more happy to find out after 5 pm when I’m off “do not disturb.” If this makes me sound like a curmudgeon, I am.

NS: I wish I could strum it like a guitar.

What sites do you have pinned to your tab bar?

NS: ProQuest Historical Newspapers.

How many tabs do you have open right now?

CH: 92… but they are nicely organized into groups that only I understand.

NS: Two. I used to have hundreds open, but it was killing my attention span, so I now make a point of constantly closing them.

Which social media platform do you use the most (if any)?

NS: Instagram, guiltily.

What is your happy place online?

CH: Browsing Sweetwater for variations of guitar pedals that I already own.

NS: Watching ukulele tutorials on YouTube.

What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?

CH: The Dato DUO synthesizer and Dato DRUM drum machine. They are the easiest way to learn to program a synthesizer, and you can’t make a bad sound. My kids jam on them every night. It’s turned them into Brooklyn DJs, unfortunately.

NS: The iPod that I traveled around the world with in 2006.

Which was the most disappointing?

NS: The minidisc player.

What game do you have the fondest memories of?

NS: Pac-Man.

Which tech trend do you wish would go away?

CH: AI music slop, full stop.

NS: Wearable computing.

What is one thing you wish you had created?

CH: In 2007 I pitched my college friends on creating an app that would allow you to legally hitchhike in other people’s cars. We started a tea company instead, which was ultimately less of a liability.

NS: Autotune.

What creation are you most proud of?

CH: Switched On Pop. My wife read this and said I should add my children.

NS: Coining the term “pop drop” to describe the instrumental postchorus in a pop song.

Which are you least proud of?

CH: My wife read this and said I should say my guitar pedal collection.

NS: Getting dunked on by YouTuber Rick Beato after calling the Jonas Brothers “stupefyingly funky” in a New York Times article.

What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?

CH: You can never have too many guitar pedals.

NS: Have a short memory.

What is your current obsession?

NS: LeBron James signing with the 76ers.

What do you do when you need to focus?

CH: Drink some tea.

NS: Step away from the computer, take a walk, and start recording a voicenote about what I’m trying to accomplish.

What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?

CH: Drink some tea.

NS: Call Charlie Harding.

When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone?

CH: During routine surgery.

NS: Whenever I go to the gym.

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

CH: The History of Sound by Ben Shattuck.

NS: Vinyl copy of the Jeff Parker IVTet.

What do you think is worth splurging on?

CH: My guitar pedals. And my beautiful wife.

NS: Fresh vegetables.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

CH: He is embarrassed there is a biopic about him.

NS: One man dared to overanalyze pop music, taking on BTS Army, Madonna stans, and the Little Monsters, and living to tell the tale.

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

CH:

NS:

Tech.title: Star Wars: Ahsoka season 2 and Starfighter get teased at D23
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Season two of Star Wars: Ahsoka is still months away, but Lucasfilm still took the opportunity to tease it a bit at D23. The company dropped the first trailer for the new season ahead of its January 20th, 2027 debut. The clip shows a darker, witchcraft-filled take on the Star Wars universe, with Grand Admiral Thrawn (blue skin, red eyes, and an unsettlingly calm demeanor) threatening to thrust the galaxy back into large-scale war after the fall of the Empire.

Ryan Gosling also took the stage at D23 to tease the upcoming Star Wars: Starfighter movie. Unfortunately, while some footage was shown, it was exclusive to those in the room, and Lucasfilm hasn’t officially released it online. There have been a few supposed leaks posted on social media, but we haven’t been able to verify their authenticity. However, it likely won’t be too long before the general public gets a look, with Star Wars: Starfighter scheduled to hit theaters on May 28th, 2027, starring Matt Smith, Aaron Pierre, Mia Goth, and more alongside Gosling.
